fields.farClip: the far clip distance, same units as nearClip - see there for the clipper that reads them. viewer_set_far_clip writes it, and saturates the x 4 global to INT_MAX rather than let it overflow when the caller asks for 0x1fffffff or more, which is a request for no far plane at all. vfx_font tests a distance against it unmultiplied. Not set by viewer_update_projection, only read there. PER MISSION, from the VIEW ('view') chunk: project_chunk_exec stores its +0xc straight into mainViewer.farClip at 0x4e755, bypassing viewer_set_far_clip. That is safe only because viewer_latch_globals recomputes the x 4 global from this field every frame. The 46 VIEW chunks in MW2.PRJ give 35000 to 250000, 50000 in nine and 200000 in seven, which is 350 m to 2.5 km in the 1 cm world unit - the mission's draw distance. 150000 in the image.
fields.aspectScale: the aspect-ratio term the projection is scaled by: HEIGHT / WIDTH x 4/3, 16.16. viewer_set_aspect_from_screen is its only writer and computes (height << 16) * 0x15555 / (width << 16) from screenModeInfo - 0x15555 / 0x10000 being 4/3, the monitor's aspect - and also stores it in screenAspect. So it is 0xd555 (0.833) at 320x200, where each pixel is 1.2 times taller than wide, and exactly 0x10000 at 640x480 and 1024x768, whose pixels are square. A port drawing square pixels wants 1.0 here. (An earlier note had only 'one dimension over another'; the direction is from the disassembly - [mode+4] is multiplied, [mode+0] divides - and screen_select_asset_variant, which matches [mode+0] against 320/640/1024, fixes which one is the width.) Everything downstream treats it as a scale. vfx_font derives the viewer word at +0xa0 as this shifted right 3, viewer_update_projection multiplies it by a factor clamped to 0x8000..0x100000 and divides the product by the viewport half-extents, and several vfx_font routines multiply shifted coordinates by it. Which of the two source dimensions is width and which is height is NOT established - viewer_set_aspect_from_screen (formerly vfx_font_sub_0148a0) takes them as param_1[0] and param_1[1] of an untyped pair - so the name says aspect without claiming the direction.
fields.centreOffsetX: a signed pixel offset of the projection centre from the middle of the viewport. CONSUMER: viewer_update_projection sets centreX = (left + right + 1) / 2 + this, read as a short, and also divides focalScale by (halfWidth + this) to index the atan tables. So it shifts the principal point sideways (an off-axis projection) and corrects the horizontal half-angle to match. 0 in mainViewer, and no writer was found, so the shipped game projects about the viewport centre. The upper half, +0x4e, is never read
fields.centreOffsetY: the vertical counterpart of centreOffsetX: centreY = (top + bottom + 1) / 2 + this, and +0xb0 is divided by (halfHeight + this) for the vertical index. 0 in mainViewer; no writer found
fields.rotation: the world-to-view 3x3. viewer_build_transform writes it through matrix_transpose, so what is stored is the TRANSPOSE of the camera's own orientation - for a rotation that is its inverse. Nine ints, which both ends agree on: the transpose writes nine and viewer_latch_globals reads nine, ending exactly where translation begins.
fields.translationX: the translation half of the same transform, written by viewer_build_transform from the last three ints of the 12-int block matrix_from_euler_order0 filled.
fields.halfWidth: half the viewport width, clamped to at least 1 by viewer_update_projection, which derives it as (right - left + 1) / 2.
fields.centreX: the viewport midpoint, (left + right + 1) / 2 plus an offset the same function reads from +0x4c.
fields.focalScale: how many screen units a world unit covers at unit distance - the focal length, in other words. viewer_update_projection computes it as zoom times halfWidth, both fields this struct already names, and the multiplicand is confirmed rather than guessed: the same local is assigned into halfWidth on the following line. The consumer settles what it means. ai_group_part1 computes focalScale times MechLoadout.range, divided by a distance - a perspective divide, turning a world size into a screen size. viewer_latch_globals also latches it into a render global. Its neighbours at +0x9c and +0xa0 are written in the same breath and are normalised forms of the same product, one with aspectScale folded in and one without, shifted so the top bit sits in a fixed place. They are left unnamed because knowing how a value is derived is not knowing what it is for. SUPERSEDED: those two have since been named from their consumers, projScaleX and projScaleY. The unnormalised y product at +0x98 is focalScaleY.
fields.focalScaleY: the VERTICAL focal length, focalScale's y counterpart: screen units per world unit at unit distance, up the screen. viewer_update_projection computes it as ((zoom x aspectScale) >> 16, rounded) x halfWidth. That is the same product as focalScale with the aspect term folded in, stored raw (0x3f18e) beside the normalised form it also gives projScaleY. So pixels are not square in the projection: y = x x aspectScale. CORRECTION: this note said '4/3 at the default'. aspectScale is height / width x 4/3, never 4/3 in any of the three modes: 0.833 at 320x200 and 1.0 at 640x480 and 1024x768, so focalScaleY equals focalScale on square-pixel modes. THE CONSUMERS fix it as the y divisor. viewer_point_above_horizon, horizon_y_at_x and horizon_x_at_y all turn a screen point back into a view ray as ((x - centreX) / focalScale, (centreY - y) / focalScaleY). Note centreY - y: screen y grows DOWN while view y grows up. viewer_latch_globals latches it into a render global beside focalScale.
fields.projScaleX: the x half of the projection scale, as a normalised mantissa whose exponent is projShiftX - the two are always set together and only mean anything as a pair. Three consumers agree and the third is decisive. viewer_latch_globals folds this into rotation[0..2] to make the row viewer_project_point dots against, and latches projShiftX beside it. viewer_project_point then shifts that dot left by projShiftX before dividing by depth, and the unproject path in render_asm_sub_03d880 and render_asm_sub_03d920 does the exact inverse - multiplies by depth and shifts RIGHT by the same amount, about viewCentreX - which is what pins this pair to the x axis rather than merely to the first matrix row. And vfx_font sets all four by hand for a fixed-scale view: projScaleX = 0x2000 with projShiftX = 3, projScaleY = aspectScale >> 3 with projShiftY = 3. One block assigning the two pairs, with y differing from x by exactly the aspect term, is the relationship viewer_update_projection builds written out longhand. NOT the same thing as focalScale at +0x94, which holds the same product unnormalised and is read separately.
fields.projScaleY: the y half - see projScaleX. Derived from zoom x aspectScale x halfWidth where x uses zoom x halfWidth, so the two differ by the aspect term; its exponent is projShiftY.
fields.projShiftX: the exponent belonging to projScaleX. viewer_update_projection produces both in one normalisation: it finds the top set bit of zoom x halfWidth, keeps a 16-bit mantissa and records bit - 13 here. Splitting the scale this way is what keeps the projection multiply inside 32 bits at full precision.
fields.projShiftY: the exponent belonging to projScaleY - see projShiftX.
fields.field_0xa8: WRITE-ONLY as far as found. viewer_update_projection stores (cosAtanTable[i] >> 13) + ((zoom * sinAtanTable[i]) >> 29, rounded), with i = min(799, (zoom * halfWidth / (halfWidth + centreOffsetX)) >> 12) - a term of the horizontal view half-angle, by its inputs. No reader: nothing in the exported C, and a disassembly sweep of the render, geometry, terrain, sim, project and ai functions for reads at +0xa8..+0xb4 hits only other structs' fields (the MechLoadout weapon fields at the same offsets). Left unnamed per the consumer rule
fields.field_0xac: WRITE-ONLY as far as found. The vertical counterpart of +0xa8: the same cos/sin atan-table combination, indexed from the +0xb0 value against halfHeight and centreOffsetY. No reader found (see +0xa8)
fields.field_0xb0: WRITE-ONLY as far as found. viewer_update_projection stores ((zoom * aspectScale) >> 16, rounded) * halfWidth / halfHeight - the zoom scaled for the vertical extent - and uses it at once to build +0xac. No other reader found (see +0xa8)
fields.field_0xb4: WRITE-ONLY as far as found. A shadow of farClip: viewer_update_projection copies farClip here, and viewer_set_far_clip writes the distance, or INT_MAX when it is 0x1fffffff or more. No reader found (see +0xa8); viewFarClipScaled is the value the clipper uses
fields.lodScale: the factor level-of-detail distances are multiplied by: viewer_update_projection sets it to focalScale / (lodQuality * 160). object_draw_lod_mesh compares a mesh's key * lodScale (16.16 product) with the object's view depth, so a narrower field of view (larger focalScale) keeps fine meshes further out, and LOW lodQuality halves the factor and switches to coarse meshes sooner. geom_poly also scales three fixed distances by it (0xe10, 0x2134, 0x57e4), which were not examined here

fields.size: the whole chunk; the installer takes (size - 0x26) / 0x97 records
fields.group: the table slot, which is also the group (star) index: objectiveTables[group] and groupTable[group].affiliation are what the installer indexes
fields.timeLimit: the MISSION time limit in seconds, copied as a full dword to ObjectiveTable.timeLimit; mission_results_update gives result 4 once it runs out, 0 or less meaning none
fields.successSound: TABL name of the table's success announcement; resolved and copied with its id
fields.failureSound: TABL name of the failure announcement; as successSound
fields.records: the objective records, (size - 0x26) / 0x97 of them; declared [1]

fields.state: 0 inactive, 3 in progress, 5 Successful, 6 Failed, 7 open for targets, 8 failed for a non-player group - see missionRecordState for the readers. objectives_draw_category (formerly objective_status_text) prints 5 and 6 by name; objective_evaluate writes 3, 5, 6 and 8.
fields.category: 1 Primary, 2 Secondary, 8 Return, anything else Tertiary - objective_debug_view's own words; the objectives screen's caller filters on it. From the static record's +0x54.
fields.type: the objective's type code, the value objective_evaluate switches on: condition types 1, 2, 8, 0x10, 0x20, 0x100, 0x2000, protect 4, timers 0, 0x200, 0x400, 0x800 and actions 0x10000..0x100000. The missionRecordState note has the outcome of each. From the static record's +0x26.
fields.prereqAll: how prerequisites combine. objective_is_active: 0 means ANY one met prerequisite activates the objective, non-zero means ALL must be met. From the static record's +0x2c.
fields.prerequisites: up to eight conditions on other objectives that gate this one; objective_is_active walks them, stopping at the first with condition 0, and objective_prereq_met tests each. Built from the static record's eight 4-byte groups at +0x30.
fields.startedAt: missionSeconds when the objective was first evaluated active, -1 until then; objective_evaluate measures the time limit from it.
fields.changedAt: missionSeconds at the last change of state, -1 until then; objective_evaluate stamps it on every change.
fields.timeLimit: whole seconds from startedAt, -1 for none; objective_evaluate compares missionSeconds - startedAt against it. A deadline for condition types, the duration for timer types. From the static record's +0x50.
fields.started: set by objective_evaluate the first time the objective is evaluated active, alongside startedAt.
fields.listed: non-zero means the objective appears on the objectives screen (objectives_draw_category (formerly objective_status_text)); action type 0x40000 toggles it. The installer sets it when the static record's +0x2a is 'V'.
fields.isPrerequisite: 1 when the static record's +0x55 is 'M'. A type-0x20 objective (objective_prereq_met) succeeds only once every objective with this set is Successful.
fields.membersPerTarget: the static record's +0x56 byte (record-relative +0x30), widened: the most group members group_assign_objective_task puts on any ONE of this objective's targets; 0 means the whole group. From its disassembly (0x24346..0x24452): EBX = this field, or the member count when it is 0, and object_test_flags only preserves EBX (push/pop, never read - hence the C's scratch_ebx argument and extraout_EBX). For a target object_test_flags says still needs work, EBX is decremented once per member whose targetPrimary (+0x14a) is that target and whose aiState is the one the objective type asks for; if it reaches 0 the target is passed over and the next is tried. So a target stops drawing members once this many are on it. The OTHER reader, group_dispatch_responder, loads it (0x240a7, [table + idx * 0xf7 + 0x9b]) only when groupCurrentObjective is the INDEX 4 (cmp at 0x24075), defaults it the same way and then only tests it for non-zero (0x24118) without ever decrementing it - and since the function has already returned when the member count is 0, the test always passes. That reader therefore gets no behaviour from it. IN MW2.PRJ (dump_objectives' quota column, 2059 objectives): 1968 are 0, 25 are 2, 8 are 3, 51 are 4, 7 are 5. PREVIOUSLY UNNAMED because the two readers seemed to agree only on 0; the second one turned out to be a gate that cannot fail.
fields.restraint: the static record's +0x57 byte (record-relative +0x31), widened: how the members this objective tasks may act on their own. Its two readers, group_apply_objective (0x23aa0) and group_assign_objective_task, map it the same way into the aiFlags they give each tasked mech, always with 0x40: 1 -> 0x02, 2 -> 0x01, anything else -> neither. The meaning comes from those bits' readers, checked directly: mech_retaliate returns at once while aiFlags & 1, and group_dispatch_responder passes over a mech with aiFlags & 3 when choosing one to send after a threat. So 0 = free (fights back and can be sent after threats); 1 = HOLD TASK (still fights back, but the group will not pull it off to answer a threat); 2 = DO NOT ENGAGE (does not retaliate either - and is not dispatched). IN MW2.PRJ, over all 2059 objectives (dump_objectives): 1704 are 0, 220 are 1, 135 are 2, no other values. CORRECTION: this note said 'installer only so far', written before either reader was traced; dump_objectives called the column aimode and said the aiFlags bits were not established.
fields.successSound: resource id (type 0xb) of successSoundName. mission_result_format, for the player's group, prints '%s successful' with text and plays this when the objective reaches state 5 - the per-objective counterpart of ObjectiveTable.successSound.
fields.failureSound: resource id of failureSoundName; mission_result_format plays it with '%s failed' at state 6.
fields.successSoundName: the name successSound was resolved from (static record +0x5a); mission_result_format loads it through dev_dir_load_sfl.
fields.failureSoundName: the name failureSound was resolved from (static record +0x65), loaded the same way at state 6.
fields.actionTable: the TABLE an action type (0x10000..0x100000) acts on: objective_evaluate multiplies it by 0x2e8a, the table stride - the 0x40000 toggle writes listed at actionObjective * 0xf7 + actionTable * 0x2e8a + 0xa57e6. From the static record's +0x79.
fields.actionObjective: the objective within actionTable that an action acts on - multiplied by 0xf7, the record stride, in the same expression. From the static record's +0x7b.
fields.text: the objective's text as the objectives screen shows it; objectives_draw_category (formerly objective_status_text) prints it from +0x95, continuing at +0xb5 past 32 characters. From the static record's +0x7d.
fields.targetCount: how many entries of targets are in use, capped at 16 by mission_record_add_value; the installer zeroes it.
fields.targets: the objects the objective is about, appended by mission_record_add_value and tested by objective_target_destroyed, _identified and _reached. 0xd7 + 16 * 2 = 0xf7, the record size. The installer writes 0x800 into the first entry (index 0, kind 8) while setting targetCount to 0, so that entry is not live.

fields.entity: back-pointer; read as loadout->entity->index and ->loadoutRating (formerly chassisStat)
fields.ramps: five interpolators, stepped every tick by ramp_step. TIME CONSTANTS, from mech_std_create's ramp_start calls: ramps[0] torso pan 0.2 s for the player's mech and 0.6 s for every other mech (the doubles 0x3fc999999999999a and 0x3fe3333333333333), so AI torsos swing three times slower; ramps[1] torso tilt 0.2 s; ramps[2] forward speed 0.2 s - REFINED: only until the first animation frame event, when mech_std_tick_ai sets its duration to 0x5b ticks (0.5 s) for the rest of the mission; ramps[3] turn rate 0.3 s; ramps[4] throttle 0.2 s, starting at the 0x400 neutral. See Ramp.duration for why these are time constants and not travel times. The array runs 0x04..0x53 and ends exactly where weapons begins. Known slots: ramps[1] is torso TILT - ai_group_part1 and damage both assign its target from control->torso_tilt, and weapon_get_aim_direction substitutes its current value into the PITCH argument of matrix_from_euler_order0, so the channel name and the slot agree. ramps[0] is torso pan, its target assigned straight from control->torso_pan, and mech_std_tick_ai compares target against current with a +/-0x20000 tolerance to play the traverse cue; ramps[1] is torso tilt, from control->torso_tilt; ramps[3].target is snapped to +/-55 degrees following the torso direction - CORRECTION: ramps[3] is the TURN RATE, not an angle. mech_std_tick_terrain does heading += ramps[3].current * tickDelta / 0xb6, so it is 16.16 degrees PER SECOND (0x10000 per degree, as heading uses), and the old +/-55 was the fixed 0x370000 = 55 degrees a second that the legs-follow-torso option (0x982ec, player only) turns at while the torso is twisted more than a degree, counter-rotating torso pan so the torso holds its world direction. Ordinary turning sets the target to (legsPan >> 10) * 90 * cos(min(kph, 80) degrees), where kph is ramps[2].current / 10000 - ground speed, 10002 being one kph. So the game uses the speed in kph as an ANGLE: a mech turns at the full rate standing, half at 60 kph and 17 percent at 80 or more. The AI's saturated legsPan of 0x3333333 gives 72 degrees a second standing; the player's full deflection, legs_pan_delta at its 16.16 maximum of 1024 << 16, gives 90 - so AI mechs turn at 80 percent of the player's best. With the jets burning it is (legsPan >> 10) * 180, with no speed term; ramps[4] is throttle or power level, its target forced to 0x400 (the control-axis maximum) whenever status is not 2, and how far current sits below 0x400 is what drives cooling in the heat field. ramps[2] is FORWARD GROUND SPEED. mech_std_tick_terrain multiplies ramps[2].current by MechEntity.headingSin and headingCos to get the X and Z velocity the mech wants, and accelerates velocityX/Z toward that over 0x2d ticks. mech_std_tick_ai sets its target to (ramps[4].current - 0x400) * speed, with a deadzone below 0x20, so the chain is throttle * throttleScale -> ramps[4] -> * speed -> ramps[2] -> velocity. While mascEngaged it multiplies the target by 1.5 for the player, which is MASC's speed boost. When MechEntity.animState is 2, the reversing state that ControlState.reverseDirection selects, the target becomes -target/2, so reverse is half speed. CORRECTION: this was recorded as 'the step bob', read as a decaying oscillation because the target is negated and halved, with the 1.5 taken as the bob growing with effort. Both readings came from the writers alone. The negate-and-halve is gated on animState == 2, and the consumer in mech_std_tick_terrain is a velocity, not a displacement of the view. The ground-contact guard (motionFlags bit 1) is real: it sets the 0x5b duration and gates the MASC branch. NOTE: 0x08 and 0x0c were first named torsoPanCommand and torsoPanActual as if they were standalone fields - they are ramps[0].target and ramps[0].current, which is why 0x38/0x3c mirrored them.
fields.weapons: array walked with stride 0x68 for numWeapons entries
fields.sections: eight MechSection records copied out of the chassis
fields.ammo: numAmmo MechAmmoBin records, stride 0x14. mech_config fills them as it walks the chassis slots.
fields.torsoNode: the torso node. Both terrain ticks stage torsoPitch, aimAngle and torsoRoll on the entity and then call scene_node_set_euler on this, guarded by a null check. FILLED BY THE MISSION FILE: it is the FIRST of the gamepiece's two THNG ('thing') chunks - see thingNodeQueue. In MW2.PRJ that is the *_HEAD part on every mech (JN5_HEAD, TW5_HEAD...), the turret on a tank (KA4TURRT) and the body on a gun turret (TA4_BODY), so it is the upper body that turns with the torso. Null for the eight VEHICLE* gamepieces, which carry no THNG.
fields.weaponAimNode: a second node, aimed at the point the weapons module computes rather than at the torso angles. The terrain tick takes the vector from this node's world position to that point, divides the vertical component by the octagonal length to get a normalised sine, and passes that through fixed_asin - so this node pitches to look directly at the aim point. FILLED BY THE MISSION FILE: the SECOND THNG chunk (thingNodeQueue). A DUMMY part on every mech, turret and Elemental, the barrel on a tank (KA4BAREL); aircraft, doors and TARANTUL name the same object for both.
fields.sectionNodes: one scene node per body section, indexed 0-based like MechWeapon.sectionIndex, so [n] belongs to location n + 1. The weapon burst loop reads it as *(ramps + 6 + (sectionIndex + 1) * 4), which is +0x68 + sectionIndex * 4, and puts the node in entity->mountNode so the shot leaves from its weapon's section. mech_jump_jet_effects reads [6] and [7], locations 7 and 8, the legs, and puts exhaust on both while the jets burn. Weapons never reach [6] or [7], because leg-mounted weapons have sectionIndex remapped to 1 and 3, the side torsos. The eight slots fill 0x68..0x87 exactly, ending where speed begins. mech_destroy_section's death path zeroes the neighbouring torsoNode and weaponAimNode, not these. FILLED BY THE MISSION FILE: each POF ('pof', tag POFO) chunk inside a gamepiece's block names a detail object and a slot, and project_chunk_exec stores that object's node at sectionNodes[slot] of currentGamepiece's loadout. The slot is not bounds-checked. A slot no POF names stays null, and both readers test for null. Plain pointers for the same reason as torsoNode
fields.speed: chassis moveSpeed scaled by 0x697e98 >> 16. UNITS, the part a port must keep: mech_std_tick_ai sets the forward-speed target to (ramps[4].current - 0x400) * speed, and the throttle channel runs 0..1024 per the game's own control table, so full throttle at throttleScale 1.0 gives 1024 * speed = move * 108026 velocity units. Velocity is 16.16 world units per 182 Hz tick: the movement step adds ((v + a*dt/2) * dt) >> 16 to MechEntity.posX/Y/Z. THE WORLD UNIT IS 1 CM, from two unrelated constants. (1) The speedometer, an unlisted function at 0x32080 that sprintf's '%d kph', takes the player's |velocity| (octagonal approximation (4*max + mid + min) / 4), divides by 0x2712 = 10002 and multiplies by the double 1.5 at 0x90cb7. One kph is 27.78 cm/s = 0.15263 cm per tick = 10002.4 in 16.16, so 10002 is exactly 'one kph' in centimetres. (2) gravity's 0x794 is exactly one g in the same units. So a chassis move of 1 is a true top speed of 10.8 kph - 0x697e98 is 10.8 * 10002.4 * 65536 / 1024 = 6913687.9, rounded to the integer 6913688 - and the speedometer shows 1.5x the true speed, 16.2 kph per point of move. That 10.8 / 1.5 pair matches BattleTech's 10.8 kph per movement point and x1.5 running rule, which may be why it is built this way; that motive is NOT established from the code. The sign comes from ramps[2].current: negative prints as reverse. MISSING UNTIL 2026-09-25, AND IT MATTERS: mech_std_create then divides this by the mission gravity - speed = (speed << 16) / gravitySetting, gravitySetting being 16.16 g - so the top speed above is for 1 g, and a mission at 0.6 g (the lightest in MW2.PRJ) runs 1.67 times as fast, one at 1.3 g (the heaviest) 0.77 times. See mech_std_create
fields.stateTimer: compared against simTick to drive the status transitions. SHARED: mech_update_missile_lock also uses this field, as a countdown in ticks rather than an absolute simTick. It sets 0x16c, subtracts tickDelta while the target stays in the cone, and adds tickDelta back while it is out. The two uses presumably never overlap in time, but nothing read shows the status code and the lock code excluding each other. A port should give the lock its own field. SETTLED: THEY DO OVERLAP, and it matters. mech_heat_update's pending-shutdown countdown (6 s from the 81 percent rung, measured as simTick - stateTimer) runs while status is 2, which is exactly when mech_update_missile_lock runs, earlier in the same tick. Starting or completing a lock during that countdown shuts the mech down at once, holding one halves the countdown, and the heat stamp stalls a lock in progress. See mech_heat_update
fields.heatThisTick: heat generated during the current tick, not a stored level. Both terrain hooks - mech_std_tick_terrain and mech_alt_tick_terrain - zero it as their first act, and the later hooks then add to it: the throttle term (ramps[4].current - 0x400) * heatDissipation / 0x2800, a weapon term of value * 0x180 * tickDelta, and a cockpit term. hud_gauge_heat_rate reads it as heatThisTick minus heatDissipation * tickDelta, i.e. a net rate. NOTE: this was called plain 'heat' and described as the accumulated quantity that heatDissipation works against. That was wrong in a way worth spelling out, because the accumulation comment read plausibly: the per-tick reset only shows up in the hook that runs first, and the hooks have no direct callers, so nothing in the call graph put the reset next to the additions. The accumulated level is heatLevel at 0x98.
fields.heatLevel: the accumulated heat level, 16.16 fixed point on a 0..100 scale. hud_gauge_heat fixes the scale by multiplying it by the bar length and dividing by 100; every other reader shifts right by 16 and compares against a small number. The clinching consumer is in ai_decide_fire (formerly ai_aim_torso)'s firing check: it computes heatLevel + weaponTypes[type].heatPerShot and only fires if the projected value stays under 0x41, so this is the quantity weapons add to and the AI manages. The same 65 threshold halves the AI's throttle in ai_state; jumping is refused above 0x27 and 0x13 in the two jump checks; and a MASC malfunction adds a quarter of the current value. THE LADDER IN TIME, from mech_heat_update: 66 percent latches flag bit 4 and a warning sound, 81 is the next rung, and past 100 status goes to 3, the shutdown, during which dissipation is doubled. The mech restarts once heat is back under 66 and 0x2d8 ticks - 4.0 seconds - have passed. Heat in comes from WeaponType.heat per shot and jumpFuel's burn, about 1.07 %/s per jet; heat out is heatDissipation per tick. CORRECTION to THE LADDER IN TIME above, which predates mech_heat_update's own corrected note: 66 only WARNS; 81 latches flag 0x4 and starts a 6 s countdown to the shutdown (status 3), which then fires even if the mech has cooled; 101 and up is the meltdown rung, not the shutdown. See mech_heat_update for the full tree.
fields.heatDissipation: chassis heatSinks times a per-sink rate. IN REAL TIME: mech_heat_update subtracts heatDissipation * tickDelta from heatLevel every tick, twice that while status is 3 (shut down), and heatLevel is 16.16 percent. So each sink sheds rate * 182 / 65536 percent a second - 0.139 %/s at the standard 50, 0.278 %/s at a cold world's 100. Ten sinks at 50 clear a PPC shot's 12.5 percent in about nine seconds. chassis heatSinks times a per-sink rate. The rate is 50 for every mech except the player's, whose rate mech_config picks from ambientTemperature AND simOptions[5], the difficulty: 140 or 70 at difficulty 0, 100 or the default at 1, and 67 / 45 / 36 at 2 for a cold, temperate or hot world. An earlier note gave just '100 on a cold world or 45 on a hot one', which is the difficulty-1 and difficulty-2 rows read as if they were the whole table. SECOND CORRECTION, from the disassembly at 0x4cd9b..0x4ce25: the claim above that every non-player mech gets 50 is WRONG. The non-player path (0x4ce0a) tests the climate too. Cold is below -30 and hot above 50. The full per-sink table is: player at difficulty 0, 140 cold else 70 (the hot compare there is dead code); player at difficulty 1 AND every other mech, 100 cold / 50 temperate / 45 hot; player at difficulty 2, 67 / 45 / 36. Slot code 6000 is a heat sink: mech_damage_slot takes 50 off this per critical, one sink at the standard rate - so at difficulty 0 a player's hit sink costs less than the sink was worth, and at difficulty 2 more.
fields.status: the mech life cycle, driven by the switch in mech_std_tick_ai. 0 just spawned: starts a randomised delay and a power-up cue, then moves straight to 1. 1 powering up: waits for stateTimer, then moves to 2. 2 running. 3 emergency shutdown from overheating, written by mech_heat_update at the top of the heat ladder: dissipation doubles while it holds, and dropping back under 66 percent returns status to 0, so an overheated mech runs its power-up sequence again. 4 destroyed: runs mech_death_update for 0x71c ticks. 5 exists too, and was missed while only mech_std_tick_ai's switch had been read - mech_std_tick_player (formerly mech_std_tick_weapons) handles it separately, arming stateTimer for 0x38e ticks and holding there before signalling the end. Besides the heat ladder, 3 and 0 are also written directly by the player's manual reactor control: a shutdown request plays cue 0xd and sets 3, and a startup request posts 'Powering up...' and sets 0. NOTE: 0 was first recorded as 'active'. It is not - it is the spawn state, and 2 is the running one. Also written as 4 beside 'Opponent mech destroyed', and sent over the network packed into a nibble. CONFIRMED, and refined, by the game's own table: mechStatusNames gives of 0, su 1, nm 2, sd 3, dd 4, ej 5, co 6, ds 7 - off, startup, normal, shutdown, dead, eject. The behaviour-derived readings of 1 through 4 were right. Two things change. 0 is simply OFF rather than the spawn state - running up from off is what a spawn looks like, so the NOTE above is right that 0 is not active, but its replacement wording was still describing a symptom. And 5, previously known only as a state mech_std_tick_player holds for 0x38e ticks before signalling the end, is EJECTION - that timer is the ejection sequence. 6 and 7 exist in the table but nothing read so far reaches them, and co and ds are not established. SETTLED since: NOTHING IN THE GAME PRODUCES OR TESTS 6 OR 7. Every typed write in the exported source stores 0..5; the three status switches (mech_std_tick_ai, mech_alt_tick_ai, door_tick_ai) are bounded at 4 in the disassembly (cmp eax, 4 before each jump table); a capstone sweep of every game function, decoded from its start, finds no mov or cmp of 6 or 7 against [reg + 0xa0]; and the one non-constant write, netplay's unpack, only relays the low nibble a peer packed from its own status (status & 0xf). So co and ds are table entries with no behaviour - a port needs states 0..5 only. What the two names stand for is still not established.
fields.blockedSteps: how many movement steps in a row have been refused. mech_move_step (formerly terrain_sub_01fca0) increments it on each blocked branch - a mech (which also records MechEntity.blockedByMech), a static obstacle, or the swept world ray; CORRECTION: this said 'both of its blocked branches', written before the three tests were read - and on a zero step while already blocked, and resets it to 0 on the step that succeeds, so it counts consecutive failures rather than a total. It is also what that function returns. mech_ai_think (formerly mission_log_sub_021510) gates the whole blocked-by-a-mech path on this being non-zero, which is what stops a single grazing step being read as a shove.
fields.selectedWeapon: which weapon the mech has selected, as an index into weapons, or -1 for none. Three modules index the array with it and nothing else does: damage reads weapons[selectedWeapon].type, the player's trigger path in weapons writes weapons[selectedWeapon] directly, and mech_weapons_tick guards on it being -1 before computing weapons + selectedWeapon * 0x68. The stride in that last one is the same 0x68 MechLoadout.weapons already records, so it is an index into that array and not some other.
fields.throttleScale: 16.16 factor applied to the throttle before it reaches the drive, so it sets how much of the chassis top speed is available. THE CONSUMER is mech_std_tick_ai: ramps[4].target = 0x400 + (control->throttle * throttleScale >> 16), rounded, and the same function then sets ramps[2].target - the forward ground speed - to (ramps[4].current - 0x400) * speed. At 0x10000 full throttle gives full speed. mech_std_create starts it at 0x10000, and a pointer-dispatched loadout reset (door_create (formerly sound_res_sub_033140)) puts it back there. mech_damage_slot takes 0x199a (0.1) off it for each of the equipment item codes 5500, 5550, 5600, 5650, 5800 and 5850 (four subtract sites; 5550/5600/5650 share one), clamping at 0, and afterwards floors it at 0x6666 (0.4) unless it is 0. mech_destroy_section zeroes it when a leg goes. So damage to that equipment costs 10% of top speed down to 40%, and a lost leg stops the mech. Which equipment the five codes are is NOT established. RESOLVED from the game's own damage callouts (damageCallouts): 5500 is the hip, 5550/5600/5650 the leg, 5800 the gyro and 5850 the engine - see mech_damage_slot for every code. 5800 also sets jumpFuel to -2, one of that field's negative sentinels. A second read in the same tick, when ramps[2].current / 10000 is 0, lets the legsPan-to-ramps[3] branch run anyway if a local flag is set and this is positive; what that flag is was not read. Previously unnamed, and recorded in mech_damage_slot's note as having no known consumer.
fields.weaponCycleLock: while non-zero, blocks weapon cycling: in mech_std_tick_player's (formerly mech_std_tick_weapons) status-2 branch both the weapon_cycle control and the pending request at 0x96200 call weapon_cycle_next (with sound 0xfd) only when this is 0. It is NEVER SET: a sweep of every non-library store to +0xb4 finds only mech_std_create, mech_alt_create and door_create zeroing it (the rest are Viewer.farClip). So in the shipped game the lock never engages. Named for what its one reader does with it. The dword after it, +0xb8, is written every tick by mech_weapons_tick with selectedWeapon and zeroed at creation, but no reader has been found, so it stays unnamed. SUPERSEDED: +0xb8 now carries the positional name selectedWeaponCopy, still with no reader - see its note
fields.selectedWeaponCopy: WRITE-ONLY as far as anything found: mech_weapons_tick copies selectedWeapon here every tick while status is 2, and door_create's loadout reset zeroes it (0x33171). A sweep of every game function for a pointer loaded from MechEntity.loadout and then used at +0xb8 finds only those two stores, and the decompiled C has no other access. Named for what is stored, not for a purpose; a 'previous selection' reading would need a reader to compare against it, and none was found. RE-CHECKED with a disassembly sweep of reads at +0xb8, +0xd8 and +0xdc in every function that also touches loadout offsets: every hit (mech_std_tick_terrain, mech_weapons_tick, player_fire_group, netplay_weapons_start_burst, mech_update_missile_lock) goes through [loadout] first, so it reads the ENTITY's field, not this one
fields.autopilotEngaged: whether the autopilot is currently flying this mech, as opposed to ControlState.autopilot which is the edge-triggered toggle request and is cleared on the same tick it is seen. mech_std_tick_ai flips this on a request and plays cue 0x1d with variant 1 for engage and variant 2 for disengage - the clearest example of what soundCueVariants is for. Moving the legs while it is set raises a toggle request, so steering switches it off; and the player's legsPan is only copied through while it is clear.
fields.jumpFuel: JUMP-JET FUEL, in 182 Hz ticks; RENAMED from jumpMode. The old note read 0x71c as a 'jump-capable' mode value, which was the full-tank value mistaken for a mode. mech_std_tick_terrain settles it (CORRECTION 2026-09-25: the burn and refill below are in mech_std_tick_ai, around 0x2808d - mech_std_tick_terrain only READS jumpFuel, as the jumpFuel >= 1 condition for firing; the fuel figures themselves stand, and the burn is also skipped for the player while cheatInfiniteJumpjets (0x961ec, the 'Infinite Jumpjet juice' cheat) is on). While the jets fire - jumpjet_enabled with loadout status 2 - it subtracts tickDelta per tick and clamps at 0. Otherwise it adds tickDelta / 4 up to the cap of 0x71c. So a full tank is 1820 ticks, TEN SECONDS OF BURN, and refilling from empty takes forty. Each tick the jets burn, heatThisTick grows by jumpCapacity * 0x180 * tickDelta, about 1.07 percent heat per second per jet. hud_gauge_jumpjets draws this value, and mech_can_jump's jumpFuel >= 6 means at least 6 ticks left. -1 and -2 are sentinels, 0x71c means jump-capable. The sentinels are now pinned from mech_config: a chassis jump value of 0 gives -2 and a negative one gives -1, each with jumpCapacity and jetDeltaY zeroed. -2 is therefore 'no working jump jets'. mech_damage_slot writes -2 for two destroyed equipment codes (5800 and 7000), and ControlState.cheatJumpjets replaces -2, and only -2, with 0x71c. What distinguishes -1 is NOT established.
fields.jumpCapacity: chassis jump value - and it is a COUNT OF JUMP JETS, each carrying an equal share of jetDeltaY. mech_damage_slot, on a critical to a slot whose code rounds to 7000, removes jetDeltaY / jumpCapacity from the thrust and then decrements this, so every jet lost costs its share and the last one takes the rest. The jump-jet cheat (ControlState.cheatJumpjets on a mech with jumpFuel -2) installs 3 jets at gravity * 3, which is 1 g each
fields.rideHeight: how far the mech's origin sits above the ground - its leg length, in effect. res_load_mgeo fills it as an out-parameter when the mech's geometry loads, so it is a property of the model rather than of the tick. The terrain tick uses it both ways: height above ground is posY - rideHeight - MechEntity.groundHeight, and landing snaps posY back to groundHeight + rideHeight.
fields.eyeOffsetY: vertical offset of the pilot's eye above aimNode, in cm - the second MGEO dword. Two consumers, both through the global pointer playerEyeOffsetY that hud_widgets_install aims at this field: the cockpit camera (camera_subject_eye_pose (formerly geom_luma_sub_0395d0)) starts its eye point at (0, eyeOffsetY, 0) and transforms it by the subject's aimNode, and weapon_build_fire_ray adds it to the fire ray's origin Y. So the crosshair ray starts where the eye is. IT IS 0 IN EVERY ONE OF THE 55 MGEO RECORDS in MW2.PRJ, so for shipped data the eye sits exactly on aimNode (the EYEO node) and both additions are no-ops
fields.mgeoWord2: the third MGEO dword, filled by res_load_mgeo from the MGDF chunk. In all 55 MGEO records it is exactly -rideHeight. WRITE-ONLY: the MGDF call (0x4f129) is the only access found - no C access, and no read in a sweep of every game function for [MechEntity.loadout + 0xd4]. Named for its position in the record because no reader gives it a meaning. A port can load it and ignore it
fields.mgeoWord3: the fourth MGEO dword; 0 in all 55 records, and write-only in the same sense as mgeoWord2 (only the MGDF call at 0x4f123 touches it)
fields.mgeoWord4: the fifth MGEO dword; 0 in all 55 records, and write-only in the same sense as mgeoWord2 (only the MGDF call at 0x4f11c touches it)
fields.torsoPanLimit: how far the torso may yaw either side of centre, in the sim's angle units. Two clamps establish it and they agree: ai_group_part1 takes the requested control->torso_pan and, if it exceeds this value, writes this value back into both torso_pan and ramps[0].target - or the negation of it when the request runs past the other side, so it is a symmetric plus-or-minus limit on the torso pan ramp. ramps[0] is already established as that ramp, since MechEntity.aimAngle is written from its current value. That it is an ANGLE and not a rate is settled by the second clamp, which runs only after testing this field against 0x1680000 - one full turn everywhere else in the sim. A mech whose limit is a full turn or more is simply not clamped, which is how a full-traverse torso is expressed. It is a property of the chassis, not of the pilot or the moment: res_load_mgeo fills it straight out of the mech geometry resource, in the same call that fills rideHeight and range. The words at +0xd0..+0xdc come from that same call. CORRECTION: this said five words; +0xd0, +0xd4, +0xd8 and +0xdc are four, and tons at +0xe4 is skipped - the MGEO record's seven dwords land at +0xcc, +0xd0, +0xd4, +0xd8, +0xdc, +0xe0 and +0xe8 (radius, formerly range). +0xd0 is now eyeOffsetY. +0xd4, +0xd8 and +0xdc have no reader found, so they stay unnamed; in all 55 MGEO records +0xd4 is exactly -rideHeight and the other two are 0. IN THE DATA this field is 90 degrees (0x5a0000) for 33 records, 15 degrees for the Kitfox and Nova, 0 for the vehicles and aircraft that have no torso, and 361 or 720 degrees for turrets - which is exactly the not-clamped, full-traverse case above. SUPERSEDED: +0xd4..+0xdc now carry the positional names mgeoWord2..mgeoWord4, still write-only - see their notes.
fields.radius: the mech's BODY RADIUS in cm, the last MGEO dword. RENAMED from range. The old note found only the targetDistance < range + 20000 test and left open whether it was weapon reach or engagement distance. It is neither. Five consumers read it as a size. mech_collide_mechs (formerly terrain_sub_0200d0) separates two colliding mechs to exactly radius + radius along the contact normal. ai_group_sub_0298c0 sizes an on-screen bracket as focalScale * radius / distance. mech_probe_ray starts its flank probes at +/-(radius - 1) sideways in the mech's own frame. mechs_blast_damage (formerly sim_objects_sub_0517c0) and environment_heat_update (formerly cockpit_sub_051d40) add it to a reach before comparing a distance. The data agrees: 170 for elementals, 450-800 for mechs, 3200 for the dropship. So targetDistance < radius + 20000 means the target is within 200 m of the mech's surface. Anything annotated while it was called range may read it as a weapon or sensor range, which is wrong.
fields.jetDeltaY: printed as 'jet_ddy = %ld'; derived from jump / moveSpeed. UNITS: the jump-jet thrust as an upward acceleration, in the same 16.16 cm per tick squared as gravity - the vertical step adds jetDeltaY on top of -gravity, and another branch of that step scales gravity - jetDeltaY, the net pull. mech_load_config (formerly mech_dump_config) sets it to ((jump << 16) / move) * 0x1e50 >> 16, rounded (0x4ceb5), and 0x1e50 = 7760 is exactly 4 x 0x794, four g. So THRUST = 4 g x jump / move: a chassis whose jump value equals its move value lifts off at 4 g against 1 g, and one with half as much at 2 g. Each jump-jet critical takes an equal share away - see jumpCapacity
fields.velocityX: 16.16 centimetres per 182 Hz tick - see MechLoadout.speed for how the unit was fixed. 10002 is one kph. TRACTION: while the jump jets are not firing, mech_std_tick_terrain accelerates velocityX and velocityZ toward ramps[2].current * (headingSin, headingCos) at (wanted - velocity) / 45 per tick, integrated over tickDelta - another first-order lag, time constant 45 ticks, about a quarter of a second, and a frame of 45 ticks or more snaps straight to the wanted velocity. It stacks on ramps[2]'s own 0.2 s, so throttle reaches the ground through two lags. Forward speed inside +/-0x20 counts as zero
fields.velocityY: vertical rate, negative downward. Besides fall damage, ai_jets_cushion_fall (formerly damage_log_fall) uses it as an automatic jump-jet reflex: below 20000 altitude, a fast enough descent switches the jets on by itself, and a gentle enough one switches them back off. (20000 is 200 m, world units being centimetres.) THE LANDING RULES IN REAL UNITS, from mech_std_tick_terrain at 0x2740b..0x27452: 16.16 cm per 182 Hz tick converts to m/s as v / 65536 * 182 / 100. Landing faster than -0x56276 plays mech_play_landing, or mech_crash_to_ground if status is 4: that is 9.80 m/s, one second of free fall at 1 g. Faster than -0x102762, 29.40 m/s or three seconds of free fall, with SimOptions.collisionDamage on, is fall damage: ((v + 0x102762) << 16) / -0x204ec4 * 50, where 0x204ec4 is 58.80 m/s, twice the threshold. The same amount goes to mech_apply_damage for location 8 and then location 7, the two legs; ECX carries it across both calls. So each leg loses 50 armour points for every 58.8 m/s of landing speed above 29.4 - in 16.16, subtracted straight from the section's armour, and armour is already multiplied by the difficulty armour scale, so the player's mech at any level, with x4 armour, feels a quarter of it. The thresholds are fixed speeds, not scaled by gravity: on a 0.7 g world a mech falls further before either one is reached.
fields.stepVelocityX: the velocity in force for the movement step about to be taken - a snapshot of the freshly integrated velocity, written immediately before mech_move_step (formerly terrain_sub_01fca0) is called. The axis assignment needs no inference: the three locals stored here are loaded from velocityX, velocityY and velocityZ at the top of the same function and put back into them afterwards, in that order. Between the two they are integrated by acceleration times tickDelta, and the matching half-step displacement, (v + a * dt / 2) * dt >> 0x10, is what the movement step is actually handed - so these are 16.16 units per tick. A deadzone snaps X and Z to zero below 0x1000 while Y is left alone, which fits Y being the vertical axis everywhere else in the sim. Distinct from velocityX at +0xf4, which is the live value the next tick reads and which the movement step can still change - the retry path doubles it. These three keep what the step began with, and mech_collide_mechs (formerly terrain_sub_0200d0) reads them off BOTH mechs in a collision, differencing X and Y to get a closing speed.
fields.stepVelocityY: vertical component; the one the deadzone does not touch
fields.flags: a 16-bit flag word. Called specialFlags while only the low byte was known; mech_std_tick_terrain and mech_heat_update both read it as a ushort, so it is widened here. 0x0004 is SHUTDOWN PENDING: mech_heat_update latches it when heat passes 81 percent, and shuts the mech down 6 s later unless 0x0008 is set, clearing it only once the shutdown has run and the mech has cooled; 0x0008 is the SHUTDOWN OVERRIDE - its only writer is the per-frame HUD dispatcher player_cockpit_frame (formerly sound_res_sub_032c50), which sets it (playing 'Shutdown sequence overridden', cue 2) when shutdownOverrideRequest is up while 0x0004 is set - and it skips the shutdown at the price of a random mech_heat_meltdown at 101 percent. CORRECTION: this said 0x0004 latched at 66 percent and was cleared on the way back down, and that 0x0008 was 'a further rung of the same ladder'; 0x0020 latches that the first leg has been lost, so mech_destroy_section can tell a second leg loss from a first and kill the mech; 0x0010 means the mech has MASC - mech_std_tick_player (formerly mech_std_tick_weapons) answers a MASC request with 'Not equipped with MASC' when it is clear, which is what gives the bit its meaning; it is set when a section slot holds an item in 5000..0x13b9, so that item range is the MASC part; 0x0100 makes mech_std_tick_terrain return immediately, taking the mech out of the sim; 0x1000 guards the overheat message so it posts once. THE MISSILE LOCK uses three bits, all written by mech_update_missile_lock every tick. 0x8000 means the target is inside the lock cone this tick. 0x0040 means a lock countdown is under way in stateTimer. 0x0080 means LOCKED: the countdown has run out, and it is cleared at the start of every update, so it holds only while the conditions do. 0x80 is the bit player_fire_group and the trigger path test before copying targetHandle into a guided weapon's lockIndex/lockType, so it is the difference between a homing and a dumb-fired missile. HIGH-BYTE BITS found by a sweep for flags >> 8 tests (the byte slip that hid WorldObject 0x1000): 0x0200 - mech_std_tick_ai returns at once while it is set, as 0x0100 takes the mech out of mech_std_tick_terrain; 0x4000 - mech_weapons_tick skips all weapon handling while it is set. No writer of either was found in the exported C (typed ORs, high-byte ORs or whole-word stores), so whether anything sets them is not established. CORRECTION, from a disassembly sweep for every write to +0x10c/+0x10d (the C hid them): 0x0200 IS written - mech_std_tick_ai sets it (or byte [esi+0x10d], 2 at 0x282a8) in the destroyed branch once simTick reaches the death timer (+0x8c), after mech_death_update has run its course; so it means DEATH SEQUENCE FINISHED, and the AI tick is skipped from then on. 0x4000 was misread: mech_weapons_tick does not skip weapons while it is set - it clears it (xor byte [esi+0x10d], 0x40 at 0x52100) and calls weapon_set_fire_group on the next weapon (selectedWeapon + 1, wrapping to 0), so it is a one-shot NEXT-WEAPON request; the sweep found no instruction that sets it. The search for a setter was then widened and still found none: or/xor/and on either flag byte, every register store to +0x10d with the instructions feeding it (0x251d8 sets 0x1000, 0x52fe8 and 0x5314f clear 0x8000, 0x2685e sets 0x2000), and every word or dword store spanning +0x10d. Only a bulk copy or a computed address could still set it, so the next-weapon branch of mech_weapons_tick looks UNREACHABLE in the shipped code. Also: mech_crash_to_ground sets 0x0100 (the out-of-the-sim bit), and mech_std_create and mech_alt_create set 0x2000 at creation (alt_create stores the whole word 0x2000); what 0x2000 means for a loadout is not established. RESOLVED - it was already recorded on MechEntity.torsoPitch: its one reader, mech_std_tick_terrain, sets the torso node's pitch to ramps[1].current (the torso tilt ramp) / 2 when 0x2000 is set and to 0 when it is not. So 0x2000 is TORSO TILTS: mechs get it at creation (mech_std_create, and mech_alt_create's whole-word 0x2000 for the static guns), and door_create's zero word leaves a door without it. 0x0001 is the TRIGGER LATCH, read in mech_weapons_tick: set when a fire control is acted on, so a held trigger acts once; cleared when all five fire controls are released (which also steps the chain-fire selection) and when mech_weapon_fire fails, so a trigger held on an empty weapon re-tries and plays the not-ready sound.

fields.handle: the open file: project_load_directories and project_read_resource seek and read through it.
fields.inUse: project_file_open skips a record while it is non-zero and sets it to 1; project_close clears it.
fields.header: the loaded header, from projectAllocHook; every reader starts here.
fields.types: one slot per header type, indexed by project_find_type's result. 32 slots; MW2.PRJ has 22 types.
fields.name: the path project_file_open was asked to open, strncpy 0x20; project_close clears it. No reader has been found.

fields.numWeapons: clamped to 10; bounds the weapon loop and locates the ammo array. THE TWO LISTS AFTER THE SECTIONS, from mech_load_config (formerly mech_dump_config)'s loops: at +0x158, numWeapons pairs of dwords {slotCode, location}, where a negative location makes the loader search the section slots for the code; then numAmmo pairs {class, weapon slotCode}, printed as 'ammo %d: class %d wpn %d', each bin feeding the weapon whose slotCode matches. In all 96 MEK records of MW2.PRJ, every one of the 221 bins has class / 100 == 100 + the fed weapon's slotCode / 100 - so an ammo slot code is 10000 + a weapon code, matching mech_damage_slot's code / 100 > 100 ammo test. tools/dump_chassis.py prints every chassis this way
fields.numAmmo: bounds the ammo loop; the ammo list itself is described on numWeapons
fields.sections: eight locations; copied out as 0x50 dwords

fields.gamepieceClass: the entity's GAMEPIECE CLASS - 1 mech, 2 truck, 3 artillery (static gun), 4 tank, 5 helicopter, 6 wanderer (unused by the data), 7 door, 8 transport aircraft - established below from its one writer, three consumers and the data. RENAMED from objectState, a name from the first reading, which took the == 1 tests for a liveness check; code annotated before this rename that says objectState means this field, and 'objectState 1' means 'is a mech'. ORIGINAL NOTE: tested == 1 before a mech is considered live. REFINEMENT, not a correction: that test is real and everything it gated still holds, but the field is not a liveness flag. ai_set_state_rule_block switches on it over the range 1..8 and picks a DIFFERENT rule-table index array for each value - six distinct arrays, with 8 sharing 5's - so it carries a category of mech, and 1 is merely the category the live tests expect. WHAT THE EIGHT CATEGORIES ARE IS NOT ESTABLISHED; no table of names for them has been found. WHERE IT COMES FROM is now established: apart from mech_entity_reset zeroing it, its only writer is the GP branch of project_chunk_exec, which stores gamepieceClasses[n].classId for the class number n in GP chunk +0xa - the same number that picks the entity's loadout constructor and hooks. So the category is the gamepiece class the mission file asked for. FOUR OF THE EIGHT ARE NOW NAMED, by the one place the game says them aloud: when an enemy (allegiance 1) is destroyed, mech_on_destroyed (formerly ai_log_new_leader) switches on this field and plays 'Enemy mech destroyed' for 1, 'Enemy vehicle destroyed' for 2 and 4, 'Enemy aircraft destroyed' for 5 and 8, and 'Enemy target destroyed' for 3; 6 and 7 fall to the default and announce nothing. So 1 is a mech, 2/4 ground vehicles, 5/8 aircraft. Why two classes share each word, and what 6 and 7 are, was NOT established when this was written; it is now. Two classes share a word because they are different kinds of the same thing: truck and tank are both vehicles, helicopter and transport both aircraft. CLASSES NAMED. The game's own names are in gamepieceClassNames (0x95d30): 0 GP_NULL, 1 GP_MW2MECH, 2 GP_MW2TRUCK, 3 GP_MW2ARTILLERY, 4 GP_MW2TANK, 5 GP_MW2HELICOPTER, 6 GP_MW2WANDERER, 7 GP_MW2DOOR. That table has NO REFERENCE in the shipped binary, so it is not a consumer; what makes it trustworthy is the data. Every gamepiece file in MW2.PRJ carries one GP chunk whose class is at +0xa, and grouping the files by class matches the names exactly: 1 every mech (and the two aircraft variants aircrf1a and aircrf2a); 2 vehiclea..vehicleh except g; 3 turreta..turreti; 4 tanka, tankb and vehicleg; 5 the aircrft files; 7 doora, doorb and doorc; 8, which the name table does not reach, dropa (the dropship) and aircrftc. No file uses 6. The code agrees too. Class 3 is the one class built with the mech_alt_* functions, a static gun, and class 7 the other special set, a door. The kill announcements say 'vehicle' for 2 and 4, 'aircraft' for 5 and 8, and 'target' for 3 (artillery), and announce nothing for 6 and 7. So class 8 is a transport aircraft, by its two files. Its GP_ name, if it had one, is not in the table
fields.index: compared against the player index global at 0x95870
fields.groupId: the '%2d' in the AI log lines; equal for mechs in one lance
fields.starSlot: star_assign_slots gives the leader 0 and the rest 1,2,3... Before that, at spawn, mech_set_star_slot sets it to the mech's order within its group in the mission file (the GPS chunk's position).
fields.controlSource: where this mech's control comes from. 0 is the local player, 1 is the network and 2 is the local AI. The values are not guessed - one statement in the mech constructor sets all three: the mech whose index equals playerMechIndex gets 0, and every other mech gets (netGameEnabled == 0) + 1, so 2 offline and 1 in a network game. The same branch is the only place hooks[3] and hooks[4] are filled in, and only the player's mech gets them; everyone else has those two slots nulled. The consumers line up with that. mech_ai_think (formerly mission_log_sub_021510) and group_assign_objective_task (formerly ai_combat_sub_024250) both run the rule system only when this reads 2, which is why a netplay mech never thinks locally - its orders arrive over the wire instead. ai_group_part1 tests == 0 together with MechLoadout.autopilotEngaged, i.e. the player's own mech with autopilot off, and elsewhere tests != 2 to mean anything the local AI is not driving. NOTE: 1 marks every non-player mech in a network game, whether a human or a bot is behind it - the field records where the input comes from, not what kind of pilot it is.
fields.flags: the most-read field. Bits 1 and 2 (mask 6) mark the mech destroyed or gone - (flags & 6) == 0 is the liveness test, and both are set beside loadout->status = 4. Bit 0x10 is cleared when status returns to 0. BIT 0x10 IS POWERED DOWN BY THE AI: ai_apply_state sets it, and ORs 3 into loadout->status, on entering aiState 10 (rest), 11 (shutdown) or -1; entering any other state clears it and sets status 0 - which is the clearing described above. THE HIGH BYTE COMES FROM THE MISSION: project_chunk_exec stores the GPS chunk's +0x22 word into this field whole (listing/gamepieces.txt prints it: 295 of 316 gamepieces 0x0400, the 16 Clan Wolf mechs 0x1400, the three Boom turrets (tur00drp) 0x0c00, the two doors 0). Its readers, all for the PLAYER as attacker except the kill count: 0x0400 or 0x1000 (mask 0x14) makes the piece a COMBATANT - target cycling skips a piece with neither (validators, -5, unless playerTargetFromReticle), and mech_on_destroyed counts a kill in the mission statistics only when one is set; 0x0800 makes the piece NEVER targetable by the player (-5, reticle or not); 0x1000 lifts the player's targeting range limit - without it ai_validate_target and ai_validate_gamething refuse (-7) a target whose slant range exceeds 0x2ab98 (175000, 1750 m if the unit is cm). So doors are neither cycled to nor counted, the Boom turrets can never be targeted, and Clan Wolf mechs can be targeted at any range. Bit 0x10 (low byte) also hides a powered-down mech from target cycling (ai_validate_target, -3, unless playerTargetFromReticle). BIT 0x2000 (flags >> 8 & 0x20): command_execute plays its UI click (sound 0xdc) for ten commands only when the player's mech has it, and mech_std_tick_ai plays sound 0x104 and cue 0x1a for an enemy mech only when it is set - both readers gate the player's audio feedback on it; no GPS chunk in MW2.PRJ sets it and no writer was found, so what it means is not established. RESOLVED by a disassembly sweep for writes to +0x15 (the C hides them): mech_std_tick_ai's status switch (jump table at 0x27764 on loadout->status) SETS 0x2000 (or byte [eax+0x15], 0x20 at 0x28253) in the same step that moves status 1 -> 2 when the power-up timer runs out, and CLEARS it when a power-up starts (status 0, 0x281a6) and when the mech is destroyed (status 4, 0x28269). So 0x2000 is POWERED UP (running): the player hears the UI clicks and the enemy cue only once the mech has powered up. The same switch also writes the low bit 0x10: status 3 (shut down) sets it and the 1 -> 2 step clears it, beside ai_apply_state's writes - which fits 0x10 as powered down.
fields.seenByGroups: bit per group, set as 1 << (mech->groupId & 0x1f) the first time a group identifies this mech. ai_validate_current_target writes it in the same breath as setting flags bit 0x20, and the two sibling branches of that function write TrackedObject.seenByGroups and GameThing.seenByGroups with the identical statement - three parallel sites is what names it rather than one.
fields.spawnDetailLevel: the detail level a gamepiece's part nodes are built at when it spawns. The GP branch of project_chunk_exec copies projectReprLevel here, the REPR nesting level in force as the chunk runs, right beside detailLevel = -1. Its one consumer, mech_create_part_nodes, reads [esi+0x18] (confirmed in its disassembly) as the level for detail_record_build on every part, then destroys the objects built at that level, keeping only the node hierarchy. The meshes come later through mech_lod_update and mech_apply_detail_level. So this fixes which REPR level's records give the part tree its shape
fields.detailLevel: which level of detail the mech's geometry is currently built at, or -1 when none has been applied - the constructor sets it to -1. Lower is more detailed: mech_lod_update ranks every mech by range each frame, gives the nearest 0, the next two 1 (and no more than three mechs may hold 1), and (threshold <= range) + 2 to everything else, so 2 and 3 are the distant tiers. This field is the cache that makes that cheap: the update compares the level it just computed against this one and calls mech_apply_detail_level only when they differ, then stores the level it applied. The disassembly settles that last step - the value written back is [ebx + 4] where ebx is &scratch[i * 3], and slot 1 of that triple is the level (slot 0 is the range, slot 2 the mech index), so what is cached is the level and not, as the bare offset suggests, the mech index at +4. CORRECTION: this used to add "viewer_latch_globals also snapshots it into a render global beside onGround and motionFlags". That function does not take a MechEntity - its first statement is viewerPosition = param_1, and every caller passes viewerPosition. The offsets it reads merely collide with this struct's. The genuine consumers are mech_lod_update and the constructor.
fields.loadout: the mech's loadout; its field 0 points back at this entity
fields.hooks: six per-mech callbacks, each driven by its own mech_dispatch_hookN that walks mechTable and calls this slot for every mech with a loadout. The block runs 0x28..0x3f and ends exactly where node begins. Most slots are handed the mech's MechLoadout.
fields.node: the mech's node in the scene tree; handed to the terrain routines
fields.aimNode: a SECOND scene node, distinct from node at +0x40, and the one the weapons aim from. Exactly two readers and they agree: weapon_build_fire_ray takes its world POSITION for the ray origin and weapon_get_aim_direction takes its world ORIENTATION for the aim basis. ai_group_part1 guards its call on MechLoadout.weaponAimNode being non-null, which suggests the two are the same node reached by different routes - that has NOT been checked. WHERE IT COMES FROM, established since: the GP (gamepiece) chunk in project_chunk_exec sets aimNode = node when it spawns the mech, and a following EYEO (eyeobj) chunk replaces it with the node of the detail record its payload names. So a mech with no eyeobj aims from its hull node
fields.mountNode: the scene node the current shot or effect comes from, set by whoever is about to spawn something at a mount. The weapon burst loop sets it to loadout->sectionNodes[weapon.sectionIndex] before each mech_weapon_fire, and mech_shot_direction takes the projectile's start from it. mech_jump_jet_effects sets it to sectionNodes[6] and [7], the legs, before spawning exhaust effect 0x19 on each. effect_align_to_mount copies its position and matrix onto the effect's node. RENAMED from fireNode, the name the previous increment gave it from the weapon path alone; that increment's guess that loadout +0x80 and +0x84 were 'at least two mount nodes' is now answered: they are the last two of the eight sectionNodes
fields.control: points at a ControlState; the AI drives the same slots the player's input does. mech_spawn sets it: the player gets &playerControls, every other mech a block inline at its own +0x1a4 that is only 0x48 bytes long - mech_entity_alloc adds exactly 0x48 for a non-player, and mech_spawn zeroes 0x48. That is where ControlState's mech channels end (self_destruct is +0x43) and the player-only half begins (pilot_tilt at +0x48, then eyepoint, zoom and menu). So only the first 0x48 bytes are valid through an AI mech's pointer
fields.posX: differenced componentwise against other positions for range/bearing. Integer CENTIMETRES, not 16.16: the movement step adds velocity * ticks >> 16 to it, and velocity is 16.16 cm per tick (see MechLoadout.speed)
fields.pitch: the body's pitch, 16.16 degrees; with heading (+0x60) and roll (+0x64) the three angles the mech's node is oriented by. CONSUMERS, from the disassembly: mech_std_tick_terrain (0x275d6), door_tick_move (0x3336a) and the netplay receive in netplay_apply_state (formerly netplay_opponent_killed) (0x44ded) all call scene_node_set_euler(node, EDX = +0x5c, EBX = +0x60, ECX = +0x64, order 0), and that function's arguments are (pitch, yaw, roll). WRITERS: the create paths read the node's world orientation back with scene_node_get_world_euler(node, +0x5c, +0x60, +0x64) (mech_std_create, mech_alt_create, door_create), and the netplay packet carries all three (dwords 10..12). mech_std_tick_terrain only READS pitch and roll. No other writer has been found, but a whole-binary store sweep cannot tell these offsets from other structs that share them, so 'set once at creation' is the reading, not a proof
fields.heading: angle units: 0x1680000 is a full turn, 0xb40000 half
fields.roll: the body's roll, 16.16 degrees - the third argument of the same scene_node_set_euler calls; see pitch for the consumers and writers
fields.torsoPitch: ramps[1].current (the torso tilt ramp) halved when flags bit 0x2000 is set, and 0 when it is not - so the bit gates whether the torso pitches at all.
fields.aimAngle: torso yaw relative to the hull: read as heading + aimAngle wherever an absolute aim direction is wanted, and compared against a bearing with a +/-0xa0000 tolerance. Written from ramps[0].current, the torso pan ramp.
fields.torsoRoll: the torso roll, and only ever written as 0. ESTABLISHED: mech_alt_tick_terrain loads this field into ECX, which scene_node_set_euler forwards as the third angle - the roll slot. The note below is kept because it was the honest reading before that was known: its position between torsoPitch and the euler call rather than from anything that reads it - nothing does.
fields.groundHeight: terrain height under the mech, from the world query. Landing snaps posY to this plus MechLoadout.rideHeight.
fields.onGround: cleared at the top of the landing check and set to 1 once contact is established. It gates the slope-sliding term, and mech_std_tick_terrain returns early for a destroyed mech only once it has come to rest on the ground.
fields.blockedByMech: the index of the mech standing in this one's way, or -1 for nothing. It is an output of the movement step, not a decision: the AI clears it to -1 immediately before calling mech_move_step (formerly terrain_sub_01fca0), and that function writes the other mech's index here - *(entity + 0x7c) = *(otherEntity + 4) - on the branch where the step is refused because a mech is in the way. The branch that refuses for terrain instead writes nothing, so this distinguishes being blocked by a mech from being blocked by the world. A plain mechTable index, not one of the (type << 8) | index handles the targeting fields use. Three consumers read it. mech_ai_think (formerly mission_log_sub_021510) acts on it only when MechLoadout.blockedSteps is non-zero, and if the blocker's mech_allegiance is 1 (enemy) it logs "Mech %2d has attacked mech %2d" with this mech as the attacker - so shoving an enemy counts as attacking it. mech_collide_mechs (formerly terrain_sub_0200d0) runs the relation backwards, scanning every mech for one whose blockedByMech is its own index, and topples it with mech_crash_to_ground if that mech is already destroyed. And AI behaviour 10 (rest) waits 0x5b0 ticks rather than 0x2d8 while anything is blocking it. A previous pass recorded that vfx_video_sub_011910 read this field as a function pointer, because its local came from a view table Ghidra had typed MechEntity **. That is FIXED: typing vfx_video_sub_0121b0's parameter void * removed the inference that fed it, and the access now reads as a bare offset on an untyped pointer. CORRECTION: that note went on to call viewer_latch_globals a genuine consumer, "it snapshots onGround, this field, motionFlags and loadout into consecutive render globals". It is NOT. Its first statement is viewerPosition = param_1 and all five callers pass viewerPosition, which cannot be a mech because viewerPosition + 0 is read as an x coordinate while MechEntity + 0 is gamepieceClass. A cluster of offsets that happens to line up with four named fields is a coincidence of two structs, not evidence - the callers are. Its parameter is now typed void *, so those readings are gone.
fields.motionFlags: the mech's motion and animation-event byte. RENAMED from contactFlags, and CORRECTED: the old note said it was 'touched only by the same landing check' and that nothing reads bit 0. The animation player writes three of its bits and two other functions read them. BIT 0 (0x01) MOVEMENT ANIMATION RUNNING: anim_player_step sets it when it starts a movement animation, there being an animState or animTarget, and clears it when the animation ends with no target; going airborne and burning jump jets also clear it. BIT 1 (0x02) a frame event: set when the current animation frame's first flag byte has 0x10, cleared as the next frame begins. While it is set and MASC is engaged, mech_std_tick_ai rolls for a MASC failure, at most once per 0xb6 ticks (1 s) and with a 1-in-60 chance (random_range(60) == 12). A failure posts 'MASC malfunction!', adds a quarter to heatLevel and switches MASC off. So MASC can only fail on the frames the animation marks, presumably the footfalls, which is not established. CHECKED against the ANIM data since (listing/anims.txt, where 'event' is first-byte 0x10 and 'step-sound' second-byte 0x08): of 194 event frames in 37 of the 38 animations, 157 fall within one frame of a step-sound frame - 94 exactly one frame after it, 34 on it, 29 one before - 26 are in animations with no step sound at all, and 11 elsewhere. So the MASC roll window mostly tracks the footfalls, but it is its own authored flag, not the footstep flag: a port must read bit 0x10 of the frame's first flag byte rather than reuse the step-sound frames. BIT 2 (0x04) AIRBORNE: set in the landing check when the height above ground exceeds rideHeight, cleared on landing and while the jets burn; ground movement (the ramps[2] speed step) runs only while it is clear. BIT 3 (0x08) STEP SOUND: set when the frame's second flag byte has 0x08, cleared as the next frame begins; mech_anim_select_gait plays animSoundId and clears it.
fields.animState: the animation state the mech is in now. It pairs with animTarget, and which of the two is current is settled by the animation player in anim_player_step (formerly project_entry_sub_01aad0): resetting the frame index to 0 also writes 0 here, and a frame flagged 0x80 ends the sequence when animTarget is -1 OR equals this field - i.e. when there is no request, or the request has been reached. The frame table carries a label byte per frame that both fields are compared against. The individual state numbers are NOT established; only that they are small and that the transition table is 4 by 4. ai_group_part1 tests this against 2.
fields.animTarget: the animation state the mech is being driven toward, or -1 for no request. mech_entity_reset (formerly ai_combat_sub_024ac0) clears this and animState together to -1, and sound_res clears it alone. mech_play_anim_transition_sound reads the pair as [animState][animTarget] into a 4 by 4 table of sound ids - base + 0x14 + animState * 0x10 + animTarget * 4 - so what the table holds is the sound for a transition FROM one state TO another, and animState == animTarget is the arrived case it special-cases. ONE STATE NUMBER IS PINNED: mech_anim_select_gait (formerly terrain_sub_01f4f0), called every tick from mech_std_tick_ai, writes -1 when the loadout's ramps[4].current is under 0x421, otherwise 0 or 1 by speed band, and then 2 whenever control->reverseDirection is set - so 2 is the reversing state. That 0 and 1 are slower and faster gaits is what the banding shows; walk and run would be names for them, not evidence.
fields.gaitBand: the mech's speed band for animation, 0 to 3: mech_anim_select_gait sets 0 when the speed ramp is at 0x420 or less and otherwise 1, 2 or 3 as speed - 0x400 passes 0x100 and 0x300. anim_scale_by_gait turns it into the walk cycle's pace: band 1 steps take 1.5 times as long, band 3 0.75 times, bands 0 and 2 are unscaled. mech_anim_init and mech_anim_clear_request zero it
fields.animSoundId: the sound id played for an animation step: mech_anim_select_gait passes it to sound_play_at at the mech's position whenever the animation player has set bit 8 of the flags byte at +0x80, from a frame's flags, and it is not -1. mech_anim_init gives every mech but the player's 0x103. For the player the ASND chunk (keyword animsound) sets it, by id or by SNDTABLE name. sound_res sets it to -1, silencing it
fields.animFrameTicks: how long each animation frame lasts, in 182 Hz ticks, for this mech. Its consumer is anim_player_step's tick: when a frame's time runs out it adds this to the task's frameTimeLeft (clamped at -this), and a zero here fails the tick with animPlayerError 7. The CONTROLLING track rewrites it as anim_scale_by_gait(gaitBand, baseFrameTicks) every time it starts a frame, so the same keys play faster when the mech runs; INIT seeds it with the unscaled base time
fields.aimRange: the WEAPON CONVERGENCE distance in cm, smoothed. mech_aim_range returns its current, and every shot is aimed at the point that far along the fire ray (mech_shot_direction), as is the AI's aim test in ai_group. mech_update_aim_range sets its target from aimRangeSeek.current each update and steps it. mech_entity_reset starts it at 50000 (500 m) with a 0.2 s time constant, so the convergence follows what is under the crosshair within about a fifth of a second
fields.aimRangeSeek: the MEASURED range behind aimRange. When the fire ray hits a mech (object type bit 0x100) or a gamething (0x200), mech_update_aim_range snaps current to the hit distance, at least 2000 (20 m). Hits on anything else, and misses, leave it to ramp_step. mech_entity_reset starts it at 50000 with a 20 s time constant, and nothing read here changes its target. So after the crosshair leaves a target the convergence drifts slowly back toward 500 m instead of jumping
fields.headingSin: sine of the mech's facing, 16.16. THE FORWARD-VECTOR CONVENTION, from mech_std_tick_terrain: the wanted ground velocity is (speed * headingSin, speed * headingCos) on (X, Z), so a mech's forward vector is (sin h, 0, cos h) - heading 0 faces +Z and heading grows toward +X, with 0x1680000 the full turn. A port that assumes (cos, sin) or a Y-forward frame will run every mech sideways. HANDEDNESS: heading increases to the RIGHT - clockwise seen from above. Proof through positional sound: sound_play_positional (formerly sound_sfx_sub_040bc0) takes (viewer - source) through vec_to_range_bearing, whose bearing is fixed_atan2(dx, dz) (0x2ab74, stored through the ECX pointer at 0x2abf7); that bearing points from the source TO the viewer, 180 degrees off the source's direction, so sound_pan_from_bearing's 0x40 + sin(yaw - bearing) is 0x40 + sin(bearingToSource - yaw). Pan above 0x40 is the RIGHT speaker - which the game itself confirms, since the weapon pan table sends 'Right Torso' and 'Right Arm' weapons (locations 2 and 5, see testDamageLocation) to 0x4f - so a source on the viewer's right has the larger bearing. With Y up and forward (sin h, 0, cos h), facing +Z puts +X on the right: the world is LEFT-HANDED, X right, Y up, Z forward, which is also how viewer_project_point maps view X to screen x
fields.targetDistance: the GROUND distance to the current target - vec_to_range_bearing's horizontal range, not its slant range, which goes to targetSlantRange next door. ai_choose_throttle reads it as the range gate - beyond twice the standoff it goes to full throttle, inside the standoff it stops - and the target validators compare it against TrackedObject.range and against a gamething's radius plus a 20000 margin.
fields.targetSlantRange: true 3D distance to the target. ai_target_nearest_enemy minimises this across candidates and rejects the winner beyond 0x2ab98, which is how it was identified.
fields.targetX: the target's world position, copied in by the validator before it differences against the mech's own.
fields.desiredHeading: heading error is desiredHeading - heading, wrapped to +/-half turn
fields.torsoTilt: current torso tilt; ai_step_torso_tilt divides it by 0xf00, the same scale the torso_tilt control is multiplied by
fields.targetHandle: the active target, in the same (type << 8) | index encoding as targetPrimary. ai_validate_current_target dispatches on the type nibble: 0x100 tracked object, 0x200 mech, 0x400 gamething. Bit 0x1000 (byte 0xdd, mask 0x10) is set when the target is dropped. REFINED: it is the handle encoding's NONE marker, the same bit returnWaypoint uses for 'no return point'. Its two writers set it while leaving the old type and index in place: ai_cycle_target when the cycle finds no valid candidate, and autopilot_drive (formerly ai_combat_sub_024ca0) when cycling nav points runs past the last one, which also zeroes the throttle. Every reader treats it as 'no target', whatever the low bits say: mech_update_missile_lock refuses a lock, the target readout in hud_target_readout_tick and ai_group_sub_029570 draw nothing, and weapons and lance orders skip it. So a port should test this bit before the type nibble.
fields.name: the mech's display name, strncpy'd 0x16 bytes out of the project chunk the mech was built from (chunk offset 0x36) with the byte at +0xfd forced to NUL. Three consumers agree it is the name and not, say, a pilot: ai_debug_sub_021050 prints it with %67.10s under a column header whose last word is "Name"; hud_target_readout_tick shows it for a locked target, falling back to the literal "Mech" when it is empty and "Unknown" when the mech is not identified yet (CORRECTION: only when flags 0x100 is ALSO set - see GameThing.flags); and lance_slot_target_name returns it as the type-2 answer of a handle-to-name resolver whose other answers are TrackedObject.name and GameThing.name.
fields.nameAlt: the second of the two 22-byte strings every named object carries. Loaded by the same strncpy pair as name, 22 bytes further into the same project record, and terminated by a NUL forced at its last byte - it ends exactly where the record does. The targeting readout displays it through the same method slot (+0x58) as name, but from a different branch: that one dispatches on the handle type to name, this one to nameAlt, and it plays sound 0xdc as it does so. WHAT DISTINGUISHES IT FROM name IS NOT ESTABLISHED - only that the game keeps two strings per object and shows them in different places.
fields.ruleSet: points at a NULL-terminated array of AiRule pointers - the rules that apply to this mech right now. ai_rules_rebuild empties it, refills it from the block in stateRules that matches the current aiState, and writes a null one slot past the last entry; ai_rules_run walks it until it reads that null.
