fields.stateRules: three blocks of AI rules, and exactly three. Each block is a ushort count followed by that many (aiState, ruleCount) pairs, and then the rules themselves, 12 bytes each, in the same order as the index. Nothing in the game code writes these three slots, so they arrive from loaded data. mech_has_rules_for_state answers whether any block carries rules for a given state; ai_rules_rebuild finds that block and copies its rules into ruleSet. CORRECTION: this was called contactLists, described as "three handle lists" whose entries were object handles, and the previous pass downgraded that to an UNRESOLVED note because ai_rules_rebuild read the same positions as aiStates. The keys are aiStates. What settles it is the caller both readings share: ai_try_enter_state passes its own second argument to mech_has_rules_for_state, and that argument is an aiState - its call sites pass the literals 0, 2 and 4, it is guarded against 0xffff which aiStateNames lists as -1 nothing, it is compared against 5 (follow), and ai_apply_state assigns it straight into MechEntity.aiState. An object handle is (type << 8) | index and so never 0, 2 or 4. Anything written while this was called contactLists, including the claim that mech_has_contact searches for a handle, is wrong in that direction: it is a per-state lookup, never a contact test.
fields.stateStack: saved (aiState, targetSecondary) pairs, pushed and popped with pendingCount as the depth. Every writer packs an entry the same way - CONCAT22(targetSecondary, aiState) - so the aiState is the low half, which is why ai_rule_pop_state takes a (ushort) of the entry and hands that to ai_try_enter_state. Naming it is what stops these accesses rendering as stateRules[pendingCount + 3], which made the stack look like a fourth rule block. The base and the 4-byte stride are established; the DEPTH is not. Two entries are declared here only because that is the region no other consumer touches. A first cut declared six, taking the whole gap up to pendingCount at +0x13c as the bound - but a loop in sim_object_dispatch_by_type copies SHORTS into +0x12c upward, so the top of that gap is either a different field or shared, and the gap never was evidence of depth. Nothing read so far bounds how deep the stack can actually go. RESOLVED: ONE. pendingCount is only ever set to 0 or 1 (ai_try_enter_state, rule action slot 2, the resets) and never incremented - no + 1 in the C, no inc/add on +0x13c in the disassembly - and both pushers write stateStack[0]; the one reader, ai_rule_pop_state, takes stateStack[pendingCount - 1]. So this is a single saved-state slot. stateStack[1] is written only by group_apply_objective and group_assign_objective_task, which store a new state at stateStack[pendingCount] WITHOUT incrementing the count - one past the top - and nothing reads it (no fixed read of +0x128 either). So a mech that already has a saved state DROPS the group order it was given: when it pops, it resumes the saved state. Whether that is a slip in the original or intended is not established; a port that queues the order properly will behave differently. Ghidra bases nearby unnamed offsets off this array, so an access written as x->stateStack + N is OUTSIDE the stack whenever N is 8 or more. +0x12c (the shorts above) and +0x19c both turn up in that shape and neither is stack (+0x12c is gpsParams and +0x19c is behindSectorClaims, both named since) traffic - read them as the bare offsets they were before this field was named.
fields.gpsParams: the eight shorts of the GPS (gpspec) chunk, +0x10..+0x1f, copied verbatim by project_chunk_exec's GPS case (the word store at 0x4fa4a) for the gamepiece it spawns. mech_ai_setup is the consumer, for local-AI mechs only: [0] low byte -> thinkDelay (0 read as 1, then + 1); [1], [2], [3] -> aiRangeOp4, aiRangeOp1, aiRangeOp2, in METRES here and x100 into centimetres there, 0 meaning 250; [4] low byte -> aiSkillLevel (0 read as 1). [5]..[7] are copied but nothing reads them - CHECKED: a capstone sweep of every game function (clib, miles and vfx excluded) finds no instruction addressing +0x136, +0x138 or +0x13a, the only access being the indexed copy loop from +0x12c, and all 316 GPS chunks in MW2.PRJ carry 0 in all three, so a port can ignore them. The block runs exactly from the end of stateStack to pendingCount. tools/dump_gamepieces.py prints the chunk side. This is the '+0x12c (the shorts above)' the stateStack note warns about
fields.pendingCount: how deep stateStack is. ai_try_enter_state pushes the state the mech is leaving and ai_rule_pop_state decrements this to pop it back. Zero means nothing saved, and the pushers set it to 1 rather than incrementing when they find it zero. CORRECTION: this read "depth of a pending queue. When it is zero the AI acts on a new handle immediately". What is stacked is an aiState, not a handle - see the CORRECTION on stateRules. The note about the storage rendering as contactLists[pendingCount + 3] is obsolete now that +0x124 is named stateStack.
fields.leaderRequest: a request a subordinate posts on its LEADER, not on itself. ai_rule_post_to_leader - slot 4 of aiRuleActions - looks up its group leader and, only if this field is still zero, writes the rule's code here and the requester's targetHandle into leaderRequestArg, so the first request of a tick wins and later ones are dropped. The leader consumes it in group_assign_objective_task (formerly ai_combat_sub_024250), which dispatches on the code - 7 takes one branch and everything else another - and then clears it back to zero. ai_rules_run also clears it when a rule's own condition code and first operand both match, which stops the leader re-running a rule it has already answered. Zero means nothing pending; what the individual codes mean beyond 7 being distinguished is NOT established.
fields.leaderRequestArg: the argument that travels with leaderRequest, written in the same statement from the requester's targetHandle at +0xdc, so it is an object handle in the usual (type << 8) | index encoding. The leader hands it to group_dispatch_responder (formerly ai_combat_sub_023ff0) for code 7, and ai_rules_run compares it against a rule's first operand.
fields.aiState: the AI state machine's current state, and the index into aiStateHandlers. The values are not inferred: the game carries its own {name, value} table at 0x95bd0, labelled aiStateNames - -1 nothing, 0 idle, 1 avoid, 2 target, 3 attack, 4 flee, 5 follow, 6 recon, 7 patrol, 8 godirect, 10 rest, 11 shutdown, 12 dead. 9 is absent from the table. That is what makes 'set to 3 when an attack is logged' read as 'set to attack', and the aiState == 12 tests all over the AI read as 'skip the dead'. REFINED: 12 is also where every AI mech STARTS. mech_ai_reset sets 12 for controlSource 2 when mech_ai_setup builds the mech, so 12 means INACTIVE - not yet woken or destroyed - rather than dead alone. mech_ai_think skips it, lance_order_apply ignores lancemates in it, and the lance menu counts them as unavailable. It is left only through ai_try_enter_state, which has no guard against 12, from group_apply_objective, group_assign_objective_task, mech_retaliate or the rules. The game's own name for it is still 'dead'. Six of these values double as the order codes the player's lance menu sends through lance_order_issue.
fields.targetPrimary: an object handle, not a bare index: (type << 8) | index. Type 1 is the trackedObjects table at 0xf8b30 (stride 0x54), type 2 is mechTable, type 4 is gameThings (stride 0x40). That is why targets read as 'index | 0x200'. ROLE, from its consumers: WHERE THE MECH GOES. ai_behaviour_wchick_tick and ai_behaviour_circle_tick drive toward it while firing at targetSecondary; ai_rule_cond_navpoint writes the navpoint it picks here; ai_ring_target_with_navpoints reads it as a tracked object; and ai_update_jumpjets aims at it when deciding the jets. So it is a movement goal - a navpoint, a formation waypoint, or the enemy itself when charging. The ai_debug_mech_table overlay prints it as the column the designers called cTgt (the player's row shows targetHandle there instead). ai_enter_behaviour copies it into targetSecondary when a behaviour starts.
fields.targetSecondary: the same handle encoding as targetPrimary. ROLE, from its consumers: WHAT THE MECH FIGHTS. ai_behaviour_wchick_tick and ai_behaviour_circle_tick aim and fire at it; mech_find_attacker reads another mech's targetSecondary == (me | 0x200) as 'it is attacking me', and mech_retaliate checks its own before turning on an attacker; ai_find_target_unclaimed counts a squadmate as having claimed a candidate when its targetSecondary is that candidate and it is in state 2 or 3; behaviour 1 'behind' takes its target mech from it; the shipped AI rules pass it (the '@' operand, @sec in tools/dump_ai_rules.py) to ai_rule_cond_target_destroyed and the navpoint and farthest-valid conditions; and stateStack saves it with the aiState, as CONCAT22(targetSecondary, aiState), so the target belongs to the state being resumed. The debug overlay prints it as aTgt. REFINED: in aiState 5 FOLLOW it is WHOM THE MECH FOLLOWS - a follow order targets agp_myleader, which ai_try_enter_state resolves to the handle of the leader - and group_retarget_secondary moves followers to the new leader when the old one dies. So what the mech fights holds for the combat states, not for all of them.
fields.loadoutRating: a single number rating the mech's chassis and loadout, stored as a ushort. RENAMED from chassisStat, whose note said only 'written from the chassis once the loadout is applied'. That was true but did not say what the value IS. mech_load_config (formerly mech_dump_config) stores the return of mech_loadout_rating here, and that function sums the tonnage, armour, internals, equipment and a per-weapon value. Its only reader is group_dispatch_responder, which sends the group member whose rating is closest to the target mech's, so the AI answers a threat with a comparable mech. Whether the designers meant it as a Battle-Value-like figure is a guess; the use is not
fields.aiFlags: a bitfield, never read as a whole number - every access is a mask. Observed bits: 0 and 1 are tested together (& 3) alongside aiState and cleared together (& 0xfc); bit 5 (0x20) is set while bit 6 is cleared in the same statement, so those two are exclusive; bit 6 (0x40) is passed straight to ai_try_enter_state as an argument, where it lands in the aiState position - see the CORRECTION on stateRules. Touched only by ai_state, ai_combat and ai_group. Bit 4 (0x10) is the one bit whose meaning is established: lance_order_apply sets it on every mech it puts under a player order (0x11 for order 2, 0x12 for the rest), and ai_run_combat_state tests exactly that bit before radioing lanceRadioMessages line 10, 'reports task complete. Rejoining formation' - so 0x10 means 'acting on an order the player gave, and owes him a report'. Bits 0 and 1 separate the two order shapes, but which is which, and what the rest of the bits mean, is not established. BITS 0 AND 1, established since from their three readers: BIT 0 (0x01) means DO NOT RETALIATE - mech_retaliate, which ai_rules_run calls first, does nothing while it is set, so the mech ignores whoever is attacking it. EITHER BIT keeps the mech out of group_dispatch_responder, which will not send it (or, as the fallback, the leader) after a target. So bit 1 (0x02) alone means 'not available to be dispatched, but will still fight back'. Who sets them: the mission file, through Objective.restraint (formerly called aimode) (1 -> 0x02, 2 -> 0x01, via group_apply_objective and group_assign_objective_task), and lance_order_apply, which gives order 2 0x11 (no retaliation) and every other order 0x12. ai_apply_state clears every bit except 0-1 when a mech in the player's group enters any state but 3, so those two survive the player's orders. BITS 5 AND 6, from a sweep of every access to +0x14e in the disassembly. BIT 6 (0x40) marks a mech ENGAGED UNDER ITS GROUP'S OBJECTIVE, and protects its claim on a target. group_apply_objective and group_assign_objective_task write 0x40 | Objective.restraint bits. Its one reader is mech_retaliate: when a mech is attacked by a target a squadmate has already claimed (the claimant is ai_find_target_unclaimed's return value), a claimant WITHOUT 0x40 is sent back to state 0 (idle) and the victim takes the attacker itself, while a claimant WITH 0x40 keeps it and the victim does not retaliate. BIT 5 (0x20) is set by group_dispatch_responder on the mech it sends after a target, in the same store that clears 0x40, so a dispatched responder's claim can be taken over. NOTHING TESTS 0x20: no read of the field masks it. The earlier 'bit 6 is passed straight to ai_try_enter_state as an argument' is mech_retaliate passing (aiFlags & 0x40), which is 0 on that path, as the state: state 0, idle.
fields.engageEnabled: whether this mech is currently allowed to go looking for a fight. Used as a boolean, and the player sets it: lance_order_apply TOGGLES it for order 3 (attack, in aiStateNames terms) - that order does nothing else to the mech except clear the low two aiFlags bits - and clears it outright for order 5 (follow). So the attack command is a latch the player flips on and off, and forming up stands the mech down. Both consumers gate the same thing on it, which is what gives it its meaning rather than just its shape: a mech is only put into aiState 2 (target) while this is non-zero. One sweeps the lance and calls ai_try_enter_state with state 2 for any mech not already targeting or attacking; the other is picking a candidate and rejects it outright when this reads zero. Nothing else in the game code touches it, so it is purely a player-driven permission - not a state the AI sets for itself.
fields.thinkDelay: upper bound handed to random_range when rescheduling
fields.aiSkillLevel: the pilot's skill level, 1 BEST to 4 WORST. SOURCE: the GPS (gpspec) chunk. project_chunk_exec copies its eight shorts at chunk +0x10..+0x1f to the entity's +0x12c..+0x13b (the store at 0x4fa4a), and mech_ai_setup (formerly mission_log_sub_021920) then copies the low byte of the one at +0x134 (chunk +0x18) here, 0 becoming 1. CONSUMER: ai_behaviour_init forces anything outside 1..4 to 1 and derives every aiCapabilities bit from it. Lower levels get more capabilities, which is what fixes the direction of the scale. The ai_debug overlay prints it after groupId. IN MW2.PRJ, over the 316 GPS chunks the game loads (walked with dump_objectives' chunk walker): 0 x36, 1 x67, 2 x51, 3 x112, 4 x44, 5 x4, and one each of 500 and 1000. So 5 and those two outliers (low bytes 0xf4 and 0xe8) are all clamped to 1, the BEST level. Whether the designers meant 5 as 'best' or as 'even worse' is not established; the code makes it best
fields.nextThinkTick: AI skips the mech until simTick reaches this
fields.aiRangeOp1: the value a rule range operand of -1 selects, in centimetres. per-mech AI RULE RANGES. An AiRule's range operand is normally a literal in metres (times 100 to centimetres), and 0 means the candidate's own object_engage_range. Three NEGATIVE codes instead take one of these three per-mech dwords, already in centimetres: -1 -> aiRangeOp1 (+0x15a), -2 -> aiRangeOp2 (+0x15e) and -4 -> aiRangeOp4 (+0x162). -3 means 0 in ai_rule_cond_farthest_valid and 'no limit' in ai_rule_cond_nearest_valid. The two consumers, which a capstone sweep of every game function confirms are the only readers: ai_rule_cond_team_target resolves -1 and -2, and ai_rule_cond_farthest_valid resolves -2 and -4. ai_rule_cond_nearest_valid knows none of them. SOURCE: the GPS chunk. mech_ai_setup copies GPS +0x14 to aiRangeOp1, +0x16 to aiRangeOp2 and +0x12 to aiRangeOp4, in metres, with 0 meaning 250, and multiplies by 100. It does this only for local-AI mechs, so for any other mech these stay 0. Named for the operand code that selects each, because that is all the readers establish. WHAT THE SHIPPED RULES USE THEM FOR, from tools/dump_ai_rules.py, where all 11 uses are listed. aiRangeOp2 is the ENEMY ACQUISITION range: every use is ai_rule_cond_team_target(agp_enemy, -2), in idle, follow, patrol and godirect, reporting to the leader or, on patrol, pushing into target. aiRangeOp1 is the same test used only in state 10 'rest', so it is the acquisition range while resting. aiRangeOp4 is a LEASH: its only uses are ai_rule_cond_farthest_valid(agp_rbanchor, -4) in target and attack, which fires when the mech's returnWaypoint is farther than this and pops it back to godirect. These readings come from how the rules use the values; nothing in the game names them. UNSIGNED: mech_ai_setup loads each GPS short zero-extended (xor eax, eax then mov ax, word at 0x219bd..0x21a00), so the 0xffff that MW2.PRJ uses in 31 leash, 35 acquisition and 17 rest-acquisition entries becomes 65535 m (6553500 cm) - effectively NO LIMIT, a leash that never trips and an acquisition range covering the whole map, not a negative range
fields.aiRangeOp2: the value a rule range operand of -2 selects, in centimetres. See aiRangeOp1 for the scheme, the two readers and the GPS source
fields.aiRangeOp4: the value a rule range operand of -4 selects, in centimetres. See aiRangeOp1 for the scheme, the two readers and the GPS source
fields.returnWaypoint: the mech's PATROL RETURN POINT: a tracked-object handle, (slot | 0x100), to a waypoint dropped where the mech stood when it broke off patrol to engage, or 0x1000 for none. RENAMED from trackedHandle, which was right about the encoding but whose note left the purpose NOT established. Its one writer is ai_apply_state entering state 2 (target), and only if the mech's CURRENT state is 7 (patrol) and this field has 0x1000 set, i.e. no return point yet: it tracked_object_creates a flag-1 waypoint at the mech's posX/Y/Z, owned by the mech, and stores it here (disassembly 0x22c9d..0x22d04, the mech in EDX throughout). Its consumers agree: mech_reclaim_waypoints deletes every temporary waypoint the mech owns EXCEPT this one; ai_ring_target_with_navpoints skips it when cycling nav points; mech_retaliate treats a mech in state 8 (godirect) whose targetSecondary is this as busy, heading home; resolve_target_designator hands it out for designator 0x2101, so AI rules can aim at 'my return point'. CORRECTION: this said group_apply_objective resets it to 0x1000. It does so only when the field is 0 (test edx, edx / jne at 0x23cb5), and the field is never 0 after mech_ai_setup - every writer stores 0x1000 or slot | 0x100, and tracked_object_remove only decrements handles ABOVE the removed slot, so 0x100 is the floor. The same dead guard sits in mech_ai_reset (0x21b0d) and ai_rule_cond_navpoint (0x21e60), and in all three the tracked_object_remove it guards gets handle 0, which its 0x100 check rejects. CONSEQUENCE, for a port: nothing found ever clears a return point once set. mech_reclaim_waypoints spares it, and ai_apply_state only creates one while this holds 0x1000. So an AI mech keeps the return point from the FIRST time it broke off patrol for the rest of the mission. VERIFIED in the disassembly: a sweep of every game function for a store, add, sub, inc, dec or bitwise write to [reg + 0x166] or [reg + 0x167] finds exactly six - mech_ai_setup 0x2194a, mech_ai_reset 0x21b1b, ai_rule_cond_navpoint 0x21e6c and group_apply_objective 0x23cc1 (each 0x1000), ai_apply_state 0x22cfd (the new handle) and tracked_object_remove 0x29e63 (dec). Code outside any recorded function is not covered. The byte at 0x167 is its type half, and bit 0x10 there, handle bit 0x1000, is the 'none' marker. The old note compared it to targetHandle's 0x10 'dropped' bit; here it is plainly 'no return point'
fields.aiBehaviour: the selector ai_enter_behaviour switches on to start a behaviour and ai_exit_behaviour switches on to end one. 0xff means none - that is what ai_exit_behaviour leaves behind. The values are not inferred: the game carries its own {name, value} table, labelled aiBehaviourNames, and ai_debug_sub_021050 looks this field up in it. The names are six-character padded - 0 stupid, 1 behind, 2 achick, 3 asrp, 4 ajmpin, 5 adfa, 6 kama, 7 wchick, 8 wbackp, 9 wpeek, 10 avoid, 11 sprint, 12 circle, and -1 is blank. The a- and w- prefixes group them: adfa is Death From Above and ajmpin a jump-in, which agrees with ai_enter_behaviour case 4 arming the jumpjets. What each name means beyond that is the game's jargon and is not established here.
fields.prevBehaviour: the behaviour that just ended. ai_exit_behaviour copies aiBehaviour here in the same breath as setting aiBehaviour to 0xff, so it is the only record of what the mech was doing last. Two consumers read it against aiBehaviourNames values: ai_group_part2 refuses a second 5 (adfa) in a row, and behaviour 10 (avoid) checks whether the previous one was also 10 before choosing its timer.
fields.pendingBehaviour: a behaviour requested from outside the AI's own decision, taken once. The consumer is ai_choose_behaviour: when this is non-zero it returns it as the next aiBehaviour and clears it, except that -2 instead calls ai_try_enter_state(mech, 4, targetSecondary) - aiState 4 is 'flee' in aiStateNames. The values are aiBehaviourNames values: weapon_fire_alert_target posts 11 'sprint' (with aiDirection) or 4 'ajmpin' when the mech is shot at; ai_behaviour_stupid_tick (formerly ai_group_sub_02d200) posts 10 'avoid' and ai_behaviour_wpeek_tick (formerly ai_group_sub_02d5c0) 5 'adfa'; the scheduler ai_behaviour_tick (formerly ai_group_sub_02c210) posts 4, -2 or a computed value
fields.behaviourTimer: simTick plus a randomised interval; when the next decision is due. ALSO used by ai_torso_scan as the due tick of its next 5-degree torso step, in the travelling states
fields.aiDeadline: a simTick deadline: written as simTick plus an interval (0xb6 and 0x5b0 both appear), tested with simTick <= it, cleared to 0, and promoted into behaviourTimer when a behaviour starts.
fields.aiDirection: behaviour 3 sets it to -1 or 1 at random; behaviour 9 clears it; behaviour 0xb fires the left jet when it reads 0 or 2 and the forward jet otherwise. ALSO the torso-scan direction: ai_torso_scan treats non-zero as sweeping right (+5 degrees a step) and 0 as left, flipping it between 0 and 1 at 45 degrees. AND, for the player's mech, autopilot_drive's saved throttle, stored every tick and restored after a blocked spell. AND, in behaviour 1 'behind', sector * 2 from ai_behind_pick_sector: the index into the target's behindSectorClaims is aiDirection / 2
fields.aiBlocked: 1 when the advance stalled (throttle zero, distance still large), -1 for behaviour 1, 0 otherwise; 1 triggers ai_handle_blocked. In behaviour 1, -1 means 'choose a sector': ai_behaviour_tick calls ai_behind_pick_sector only while it is -1 and then sets it to 0. autopilot_drive also uses it for the player's mech: it sets 1 while ai_handle_blocked reports an obstacle, and on the next clear tick restores the throttle saved in aiDirection and clears it. CORRECTION to '1 when the advance stalled (throttle zero, distance still large)': in behaviour 1 the large value is the heading error to the enemy - 1 means the mech has reached its waypoint and is TURNING TO FACE (ai_pursue_target_guarded); it goes back to 0 when the waypoint is more than 45 m away. ai_exit_behaviour and ai_enter_behaviour both zero it
fields.avoidObstacle: the obstacle the mech is currently steering around, or null when there is none. Typed WorldObject * because ai_group compares it directly against what object_node_userdata returns, which is a scene node userdata - two things compared with == are the same type. The debug overlay reading avoidObstacle + 2 through altTypeLetters agrees: +2 is WorldObject.type, and those letters are its class bits.
fields.avoidNextCheck: the simTick before which ai_handle_blocked will not look again. It returns the obstacle it already had rather than casting fresh rays while simTick is below this, and sets it on the way out: simTick + 10 for the player's own mech, and for everyone else simTick + 0xb6 with nothing in the way or simTick + 0x5b while avoidObstacle is set. That last pair is the whole of the "thinks twice as often while avoiding" behaviour, and the player being checked every 10 ticks regardless is what keeps his own obstacle read current.
fields.avoidTurnSign: which way round avoidObstacle to go - the value turn_sign_toward returned, with 0 meaning no avoidance is in progress. Latching it is what stops the mech dithering: it is only chosen when it is still 0, so the side picked on the first frame is kept until the obstacle clears. The pilot casts its follow-up probe with the sign negated, and ai_update_jumpjets (formerly ai_update_advance) refuses the turn-to-face path (the one aiCapabilities bit 0 gates) while this is non-zero, so avoiding takes precedence over aiming.
fields.avoidProbeScale: how far ahead to look for an obstacle, as a 16.16 scale that ai_handle_blocked multiplies by 5000 to get the length of each probe ray - so the floor of 0x4ccc, just under 0.3, is a minimum reach of about 1500 units. It is recomputed only when a fresh avoidance starts, i.e. while avoidTurnSign is still 0, and then held for all four probe angles of that sweep. It is derived from SPEED: the octagonal magnitude of MechLoadout.velocityX and velocityZ - the horizontal pair, by the same max + (mid + min) / 4 approximation ray_normalise uses - shifted left 0x10 and divided by 500000. So a mech looks further ahead the faster it is going. A mech whose gamepieceClass is not 1 gets half the reach.
fields.behaviourCommitted: set while the running AI behaviour is one that must not be second-guessed. ai_enter_behaviour zeroes it on every entry and sets it to 1 for behaviours 4 'ajmpin', 5 'adfa', 9 'wpeek' and 11 'sprint' (aiBehaviourNames). THREE CONSUMERS, each backing off while it is set: ai_update_jumpjets does not switch the jump jets off; ai_blocked_ends_behaviour, and the same test inlined in ai_choose_behaviour, do not treat a blocked mech as stuck, so it neither ends the behaviour nor picks 10 'avoid'; and ai_behaviour_tick's out-of-weapons rule does not post a flee or kama. The name is what the three readers have in common; four behaviours set it, and two of them (ajmpin, sprint) visibly drive the jets themselves. Why wpeek and adfa need it is not established
fields.targetDistanceAtDecision: snapshot of targetDistance taken when a behaviour is entered
fields.aiCapabilities: a bitmask of the AI moves this mech's pilot is allowed to make, DERIVED FROM aiSkillLevel by ai_behaviour_init (level 1 best): bit 0 and bit 1 for levels 1-3, bit 2 for levels 1-2, bit 3 for any mech in gamepieceClass 1, bit 4 always, bit 5 for level 1 in gamepieceClass 1 only, bit 6 always. WHAT THE BITS GATE: bit 0 (1) lets ai_update_jumpjets switch the jump jets on to reposition when the target is outside the torso arc; bit 1 (2) permits the jump evade, the sole extra condition on requesting behaviour 4 'ajmpin' (also in weapon_fire_alert_target, on the mech being shot at); bit 2 (4), tested on the SHOOTER, lets weapon_fire_alert_target warn its target of incoming guided or PPC fire on a 2-in-3 roll, which can make the target sprint or jump away (CORRECTION: this said the bit 'is about choosing a weapon' - the 0x58-stride read is WeaponType.guided of the weapon being fired); bit 4 (0x10) guards a call to ai_has_line_of_fire (formerly ai_group_sub_02bf20) taken only after ai_decide_fire (formerly ai_aim_torso) succeeds - the line-of-fire test: with the bit set the AI holds fire unless its torso faces the target and a ray to it is clear (it is set for every skill level); bit 5 (0x20) is what lets a disarmed mech pick behaviour 6 'kama' in ai_behaviour_tick's out-of-weapons rule. So only the best pilots go kamikaze. No test of bits 3 or 6 has been found. CORRECTION: this note said 'Nothing in the decompiled code writes it - all five accesses are tests - so it arrives with the mech from loaded data', and that bit 3 and everything above bit 4 are never tested. Both were wrong. The writer, ai_behaviour_init, stores through a pointer the decompiler did not tie to the entity, so a search for the field name missed it; and bit 5's test sits in ai_behaviour_tick as a raw byte access. The bit meanings above are still described by what they gate, not by a trait name from the game.
fields.behindSectorClaims: how many AI mechs are currently using each of the eight 45-degree sectors around THIS mech, sector 0 in front of it and 4 behind, for behaviour 1 'behind'. Consumer: ai_behind_pick_sector reads the target's counts and picks the first free sector on the flank or rear. Writers: ai_behaviour_tick's behaviour-1 branch increments the target's byte at aiDirection / 2 when it commits and decrements the old one first; ai_exit_behaviour decrements the held one when behaviour 1 ends, if targetSecondary is a mech handle (0x200). The behaviour-state reset (ai_behaviour_init (formerly ai_group_sub_02c5f0)) memsets all 8 to 0. It ends exactly at the entity's end, 0x1a4. This is the +0x19c the stateStack note warned renders as stateStack + 0x78

fields.digDriver: the Miles DIG driver sound_install_dig_driver (formerly sound_config_sub_044020) returned; sound_init frees the block and fails when it is 0
fields.sampleHandles: HSAMPLE per channel: sound_init allocates channelCount of them; channels 8..15 are filled by sound_emitter_update with AIL_allocate_file_sample and zeroed by sound_emitter_stop. voice_line_start copies the voice channel's into voiceSample
fields.channelCount: sound_init's argument clamped to 16 (sound_init_all passes 8), lowered to the number of handles and buffers actually allocated; sound_sample_open and sound_refill_buffers scan only these
fields.inUse: 1 while the channel is playing: set by sound_channel_start and sound_emitter_update, cleared by sound_sample_eos, by a steal in sound_sample_open and by sound_stop_channels. sound_sample_open's default user-data 0 points here, so the EOS callback's final store clears it too
fields.headers: the 14-byte SFLX header per channel (stride 14): 'SFLX', an unread size, the block count at +8 and samples per block at +0xc; sound_sample_open copies it and compares the tag
fields.blocksLeft: blocks not yet decoded; sound_refill_buffers subtracts each chunk and loads a 0-length buffer (end of stream) once it is 0
fields.blocksPerHalf: 0x2000 / blockLen - the blocks one half buffer holds
fields.chunkBlocks: min(blocksPerHalf, the header's block count): what each refill decodes while more remain
fields.halfBytes: blockLen * blocksPerHalf: the second half buffer starts this far into the 0x4000-byte allocation, and a full refill loads this many bytes
fields.halfBuffers: two pointers per channel (stride 8): [0] the malloc(0x4000) from sound_init, [1] = [0] + halfBytes, set by sound_sample_open
fields.data: read pointer into the SNDS resource (or caller buffer), past the header; advanced by each decode, and 0 when there is none
fields.startTick: simTick at sound_channel_start plus its delay when that exceeds tickDelta; sound_refill_buffers leaves the channel alone until simTick reaches it
fields.bearing: the source azimuth sound_channel_start stored; used for the pan when pan is -1
fields.pan: Miles pan 0..0x7f (0x40 centre), or -1: sound_refill_buffers then takes sound_pan_from_bearing(bearing) at every refill
fields.volume: volume * scale (16.16, rounded) from sound_channel_start; voice_resume rewrites the voice channel's; set on the sample at every refill
fields.soundId: the SNDS id playing (-1 for a caller buffer), compared by sound_sample_open's 0x200/0x400 rules; cleared by sound_sample_eos and sound_emitter_stop
fields.flags: low byte the priority (a busy channel is stolen by a request whose whole 16-bit flags word exceeds it, so any request with a high-byte flag outranks every priority); high byte: 0x100 RESERVED - never free or stolen, and a second 0x100 request is refused (the voice channel, 0x150); 0x200 a new request for the same id ends and reuses this channel; 0x400 a new request for the same id is refused; 0x1000 set by the emitters (looping file sample), and makes sound_sample_eos repeat a chained id

fields.name: what a path task names in its argument string; task_object_track strcmps against it
fields.pointCount: (chunk size - 0x48) / 0x1c. task_object_track treats reaching pointCount - 1 as the end of the path
fields.points: 64 slots - the stride leaves room for exactly that. path_table_load's guard is count < 0x41, so a 65-point PTBL would be accepted and its last point would overwrite the next path's name

fields.count: how many objectives are live: (MTBL chunk size - 0x26) / 0x97, one per static record. The record loops bound on it.
fields.startTime: missionSeconds when objective_table_start ran, -1 at install.
fields.decidedAt: missionSeconds when mission_results_update decided the result, -1 at install.
fields.timeLimit: seconds from startTime; mission_results_update gives result 4 (out of time) once it is reached, and 0 or less means no limit. From the MTBL chunk's +0xc.
fields.successSound: resource id (type 0xb) of the chunk's +0x12 name, the one ending in S; mission_result_text plays it beside 'Mission successful'.
fields.failureSound: resource id of the chunk's +0x1d name, the one ending in F; mission_result_text plays it beside 'Mission failed'.
fields.successSoundName: the name successSound was resolved from; mission_result_text loads it with dev_dir_load_sfl beside 'Mission successful'.
fields.failureSoundName: the name failureSound was resolved from, loaded the same way beside 'Mission failed'.
fields.result: the table's overall mission result, 0 in progress, 2 successful, 3 failed, 4 out of time - see the objectiveTableResult note, which is this field of table 0.
fields.affiliation: the group's affiliation, copied from groupTable at install.
fields.objectives: the objective records; missionRecordState labels the first of table 0.
